maintopic: FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1954-55 WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT ON GRAIN FOR 1956-57

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Irvin Sluder (Swift Current-Maple
Creek): Mr. Speaker, I wish to submit a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, of which I have given him previous notice, hoping he could, if possible, answer it today.
Is the minister in a position to announce the final payment on wheat through the wheat board for the 1954-55 crop year? Can he also inform us what the initial payment on grain will be during the new 1956-57 crop year?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1954-55 WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT ON GRAIN FOR 1956-57
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having received notice of the question I have been able to get certain information and can make a statement to the house concerning three aspects of the western grain marketing situation: one, the final payment on the 1954-55 wheat pool account; two, the policy of the wheat board with respect to delivery quotas during the remainder of the present crop year; three, initial prices for wheat, oats and barley during the crop year which begins August 1 next.
Dealing first with the final payment covering the 1954-55 pool account wheat, I am pleased to be able to advise the house that the Canadian wheat board propose making a cut-off as at May 4, tomorrow, and are recommending to the government a transfer of the unsold stocks, approximately 50 million bushels in amount, to the 1955-56 pool account as at that date. This action will enable the board to close out the 1954-55 pool account.
Total receipts of wheat from producers in this pool amounted to 318,439,061 bushels plus 615,839 bushels purchased from other than producers and 164,055,511 bushels transferred from 1953-54 pool account, a total of 483,110,411 bushels.
As soon as the board's accounts have been completed, I shall be in a position to announce to the house the exact amount of the final payment and the rate per bushel for each grade of grain delivered to the pool. I expect to be in a position to make this announcement about the middle of this month. According

Inquiries of the Ministry to present plans, the wheat board will begin issuing cheques to producers on or about May 22 or 23 and will have completed this final payment about the end of this month of May.
I turn now to policy with respect to delivery quotas at country points. A very heavy movement of wheat and other grain into and out of country elevators is now under way. Deliveries by farmers will increase as road conditions improve and will continue at a high level during the balance of the current crop year. The movement of grain to seaboard is also very heavy. Our export clearances are now reflecting heavy sales commitments entered into in recent months, about which I have previously informed the house. I am not yet in a position to put a firm estimate on export clearances for the whole of the crop year but I can assure hon. members that wheat and flour export clearances will substantially exceed last year's figure of about 252 million bushels.
As a result of this heavy outward movement, the wheat board has been able to increase its grain delivery quotas very substantially in recent weeks. As at May 1 only 14 stations remained on a quota of 1 bushel per specified acre. A 2-bushel quota is in effect at 478 stations. Some 572 stations have a 3-bushel quota, 602 stations a 4-bushel quota and 400 stations a 5-bushel quota. In addition to these basic quotas, supplementary quotas are in effect covering delivery of malting barley, high grade oats, rye and various classes of seed grain. Since the beginning of the season an open quota has been in effect covering the delivery of Durum wheat and flaxseed.
Total grain deliveries since August 1 are now about 300 million bushels and the Canadian wheat board expects that space will be provided at country elevators to enable total farm deliveries * of about 500 million bushels during the crop year. It is expected that wheat deliveries for the whole of the present crop year will exceed 1954-55 but that deliveries of oats and barley will fall somewhat short of last year's figure.
I have, been advised by the board that although they expect that they will be in a position to accept delivery from producers of as much grain as in 1954-55, it may not be possible for them to arrange to equalize deliveries by individual farmers to the extent that this was arranged for during the past two crop years. Hon. members may remember that during last crop year the board endeavoured to provide delivery opportunities to enable all producers to deliver a minimum quota of eight bushels per specified acre. This looked like a feasible target.


However, estimates of potential deliveries at many delivery stations proved to be wide of the mark, and it was not possible for the board to accept all the eight-bushel deliveries prior to July 31. It therefore became necessary for the board to issue special 1955-56 quota delivery permits to enable producers who had not delivered their eight-bushel quota prior to July 31 to complete these deliveries along with new quota deliveries during the current season.
It is always the aim of the board to equalize delivery opportunities in so far as this is possible. The board has advised me, however, that last year the attempt to reach a uniform target did have an adverse effect upon the marketing of Canadian grain in export markets. Much of the grain delivered last fall against the previous year's quota and moved to terminal positions was made up of varieties and grades not needed for immediate marketing requirements. This grain added to the congestion in storage facilities and utilized scarce transportation, thus creating difficulties for the board in moving to seaboard position for immediate clearance those varieties and grades of new crop grain for which there was an immediate and urgent demand.
In the light of this experience the Canadian wheat board have advised me that, if they are to meet market requirements and their forward sales commitments, it may not be possible to attain a uniform quota at all delivery stations during the present crop year.
The primary objective of the board will be to bring forward grain to cover sales commitments or for which there appears to be a ready demand. The board will, however, working with the transport controller, the elevator companies and the railways, continue to endeavour to achieve as high a degree of equality of delivery opportunity as is possible without interfering with the sales objective. The board will increase delivery quotas at individual stations as space is created, but will restrict shipments of grain from higher quota stations to the movement of grain required to meet commitments. In order to avoid the serious situation that arose last year, the wheat board has decided that all quotas in effect as at July 31, 1956, will expire as at that date and deliveries after August 1 will apply against the 1956-57 crop year quotas which will be made effective on August 1.
Although this wheat quota policy may result in some producers in western Canada, at the end of the current crop year, having delivered more grain per specified acre than others, there should be general agreement

that, at a time of intense international competition, the Canadian wheat board must have freedom to give preference to deliveries of the varieties and grades of grain for which there is an immediate demand and that the board cannot afford to pass up market opportunities in an endeavour to equalize farm deliveries between producers.
At this time, I also wish to announce to the house that the government has approved initial prices to be paid by the Canadian wheat board on the basic grades of wheat, oats and barley for the crop year beginning August 1, 1956, at the same level as during the present crop year. These initial prices are as follows:
Wheat-$1.40 per bushel basis No. 1 Manitoba Northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver.
Oats-65 cents per bushel No. 2 Canada Western in store Fort William/Port Arthur.
Barley-96 cents per bushel basis No. 3 Canada Western six-row in store Fort William/Port Arthur.

Supply-Agriculture SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Administration service-
1. Departmental administration (including advisory committee on agricultural services), $670,015.

In taking part in the debate on the agriculture estimates, it is not my intention to take up too much time, and I do not believe I shall take my full allotted time of 30 minutes. Nor shall I give what might be termed a statistical address, offering a multitude of figures that I know few people care to listen to and even fewer people care to read. I shall leave that to the Minister of Agriculture, who is a past master in the art of conglomerating and twisting figures and statistics to suit the immediate occasion. Nobody knows what they are all about; perhaps not even the minister. It all simmers down to a little bit of addition here and a little bit of subtraction there with even some multiplication and division thrown in, and I am sure that in order to make the farmers appear better off than they ever have been he must have used much more addition than subtraction. We have been told of meetings held across western Canada in protest against the government's wheat policy. On reviewing the proceedings and statements made by different members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at their meeting in Hamilton one sees that the same thing could very easily happen in eastern Canada. I should like to quote a few extracts from what was said at that meeting. In the Rural Co-operator of January 31, 1956 I find the following:
The federal minister of agriculture is trying to "make fools out of the farmers of this country'', D. E. Stauffer, a past president of United Cooperatives of Ontario, told the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Hamilton on January 25. Mr. Stauffer urged the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to protest strongly the misleading impressions of farm prosperity given by published reports of a January 23 speech of the Canadian Minister of Agriculture.
Again I quote:
The C.F.A. annual meeting on January 26 approved a statement noting "with regret" that the minister's comparison of cash and net farm income for the most recent five year periods "while technically correct tends to leave an erroneous impression with the public."
I quote further:
"How long is Mr. Gardiner going to be allowed to get away with this kind of thing", Mr. Stauffer asked. "A whole year's work is thrown away when the minister gives statements like that to the press. He does it every year before the C.F.A. meeting, and it's got to stop."

Eastern members have listened very attentively and, I may say, with a great deal of interest and sympathy to the debate with relation to the difficulties of the prairie farmers which has taken up much of the time of the house since January 10. After listening to the debate yesterday on the distribution of box cars I am beginning to wonder whether there has not been a word spoken in the house for every grain of surplus wheat there is in the western provinces.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether we could have a little order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is very difficult to hear the hon. member. At the same time, if he did not refer so extensively to his notes perhaps he might himself command a little better order in the chamber.
Hear, hear.
That is a fine bunch to be applauding.
I am referring to notes and I have noticed that many hon. members on the other side of the house, especially the cabinet ministers on the front bench, refer to notes all the time.
They read their entire speeches.

We fully appreciate the fact that many hundreds of farmers in the three prairie provinces are experiencing very difficult times. It is no secret, it is a known fact to everyone that the whole economy of the west depends on the prosperity of those living in the rural districts and their ability to dispose of their wheat or at least to deliver a sizeable quantity of their crop to the elevator.
From listening to different members and looking over reports concerning the prairies we know that there are many millions of bushels of wheat still on the farm and that many hundreds of farmers have received very little and in some cases no cash for their crop for a year or more. Is it any wonder that the farmers are not only asking for but demanding, although in vain, cash advances on farm stored grain? I admit that guaranteed bank loans will be of some help. That is why we the official opposition supported the resolution; but it will not solve the financial difficulty and stress that many producers find themselves in at the present time. The wheat they have in storage on their farms is in fact equivalent to their hard-earned dollars of the past year, and in some instances for a longer period. No wonder they object to paying interest on

their own money. I have been in communication with many western wheat growers and they seem to be all of the same opinion, regardless of their political affiliations, namely that the wheat board should advance them cash on the grain stored on their farms.
While western agriculturists at the present time are subjected to all this difficulty, that is not saying that everything in eastern Canada is rosy; not by any means. The farmer in eastern Canada-and I have in mind now the dairy farmer-has his many problems owing to reduced revenue and rising cost. The dairy farmers in eastern Canada would and could feed many millions of bushels of western grain if they could get for their milk products a remuneration comparable to the cost of grain they buy. Every farmer is well aware of the fact that if he purchases feed grain at $3 per hundred, which is the price in the east at present, and has been for quite some time, he must receive the same price per hundred for his milk in order to make it profitable for him to purchase. Today the farmer who is producing milk for butter, evaporated or powdered milk or cheese receives from $2 to $2.40 per hundred net. Hence it is utterly impossible for him to buy grain at $3 per hundred and receive an average of approximately $2.25 for his products.
At this time I should like to give some statistics with regard to the price paid in one of the three concentrated milk plants in my own county in order to show the committee the difference in price of milk at the present time as compared with that in 1951. In 1951 the top price in this one particular milk plant was $3.25 per hundred with a low price of $3.15. I am taking the lowest price paid that year. In 1952 the price dropped to $2.75 or a drop of 40 cents per hundred. In 1953 the price dropped again to $2.33 per hundred or a net drop of 82 cents from 1951. In 1954 the price dropped to $2.34 per hundred or a net drop of 81 cents from 1951. In 1955 the price was $2.43 or a drop of 72 cents from 1951.
Taking into consideration the total number of pounds of milk shipped to this milk plant in those four years, the net loss to the shippers to that plant was $1,322,653 or a net loss per year of an average of $330,000.
In my county we have three milk plants of practically comparable size. Therefore the loss to the dairy farmer in Leeds county, or its borders, in the three milk plants is $1 million per year. Cheese also is an important product in my county, as well as in other parts of eastern Canada-as you know, eastern Ontario has the banner cheese-producing county in Canada, Things are not altogether 67509-224
Supply-Agriculture
rosy for the cheese producer either. In 1951 the average price for cheese milk was $2.74 per hundred. In 1952 it was $2.16; in 1953, $2.14; and in 1954, $2.20. When you take into consideration the amount of milk that is purchased in Ontario to make cheese you will see that the loss in those four years was $3,625,200 annually. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, that proves conclusively to me that there has been a reduction in the purchasing power of the dairy farmers of Ontario, particularly of eastern Ontario.
I say to my western friends, if we in the east were to receive a fair and comparable price for our produce we could take care of many, many millions of your western grain surplus. In fact, we would have to increase the grain rations to our herds of cattle by an average of only three or four bushels a day for each farm to take care of a least 50 million bushels of your surplus. I have heard many farmers make the statement that they would like to feed their cattle, especially the dairy cows, more grain but they could not afford to purchase it.
Few people who have not had the experience can visualize the overhead cost of a dairy farmer. He must provide storage for his hay, grain and silage and stables for his cattle. The cost is terrific and now that farm labour is so scarce he must have his farm well-equipped with machinery, not only seeding and harvesting equipment but very expensive machinery for his forage crops such as hay and corn. This runs into many thousands of dollars.
If a young professional man, or a man working in industry at a fair salary or wage, wants to build or purchase himself a house he can get a loan from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation up to 90 per cent of the value, but if a young man wants to purchase a farm he can get a loan of only 60 per cent of the value from the farm loan board. Why is this? Why the discrimination? It must be that the government thinks the earning power of the man in business, or the man who works in industrial plants, is greater and more secure than that of the man on the farm. If this is so, it is about time they gave some consideration to the needs of agriculture so that the earning power of the farmer will be equal to that of people in other walks of life.
A young man may buy a farm now with the ordinary down payment, and by the time he gets it stocked with cattle and equipped with the necessary implements and before the mortgage is discharged, he has paid the equivalent of the amount of the mortgage two or three times in interest and, in many instances, at his death he is compelled to leave a portion of the mortgage for his son

Supply-Agriculture
to finish paying. That has happened quite often. Is it any wonder that the farmers' sons are not staying at home to carry on where their fathers leave off? I hope the time will not come when it will be the survival of the largest. Surely there is a place in our rural districts for small-sized family farms; but I am afraid they are fast disappearing. Why? Because the farmer and his son or help, whichever it may be, on the ordinary farm cannot make his revenue meet his expenses.
Farmers to the number of 205,000 filed income tax returns for 1953 showing an average net income of $2,125. Of this number, 135,000 with an average income of only $1,244 were not taxable. Those who do file income tax returns are the largest and most successful farmers, and yet they earn only an average income of $2,125. But that is not all. We must realize that it is not the farmer or the head of the house, who earns this income; it is the earnings of the whole family, his wife and family combined. I think it is high time that the farmer's wife, who works long hours on the farm and helps her husband and looks after the family, should be allowed $250 as an exemption in income tax as are other wives who work in offices, shops or factories.
Then, there is the smaller farmer, his wife and family, who are earning an average of only $1,244 or less. A man who is slightly handy can go down town and buy himself a hammer, a saw and an old rusty square and earn far more as a carpenter's helper, working only eight hours a day, five days a week, than he can on the farm at the present time.
Whenever the Minister of Agriculture speaks he always averages the years 1951, 1952, 1953, 1954 and 1955. He is very careful not to present the economic picture of the last three years when the net farm income declined around 60 per cent. I have a machine price list in my hand. In 1941 a binder could be purchased for $253.50. At the present time anybody who has had anything to do with farming and with farm machinery knows that the price has more than doubled. At the present time we pay $550 for a binder. There has been an increase from $253.50 in 1941 to $550 at the present time. That goes for all. kinds of machinery that the farmer must buy to carry on his farming activities. It is not so much the number of dollars a farmer owns, it is the purchasing power of those dollars that count.
In 1901 the farm population was 45 per cent of the total population. In 1951 it was only 19 per cent. But the lamentable part
[Mr. Stanton.1
of the story is that 19 per cent of our population today is receiving only 6-8 per cent of our gross national income, which is out of all proportion. In fact, from 1951 to 1954 the farmer's share of the gross national income has dropped from 13-6 per cent to 6-8 per cent, and still the minister has the audacity to tell the house and every public meeting that he addresses that there is nothing wrong with agriculture.
There were more unpaid taxes in the rural municipalities of eastern Ontario in 1955 than there had been for many years, and I presume that is true of all farming districts of Canada. Also, many grocery and hardware stores in the rural villages are going on a cash basis, which is a very good criterion of the diminishing purchasing power of the farmers.
It has been so long since eastern Canada has had a minister of agriculture that we in the east are beginning to wonder whether the minister is of the opinion that there are no farmers in the east at all. I believe we have not had a minister of agriculture in eastern Canada since 1911. If the Conservative party does not appoint one from eastern Canada after the next election-surely we are entitled to one in every 50 years-they will certainly hear from me.
The heads of the different agricultural associations have been doing a wonderful job in creating better public relations between the urban and rural districts. They have gone a long way in dispelling the suspicion that the farmer was getting too much for his products. Now the minister runs around telling how well off the farmers are, how much better off they are now than they were years ago. He does more harm in one of his speeches that is broadcast on the radio and printed in the press than the public relations association can rectify in a whole year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And he does it just about once a week.

Mr. Chairman, in my constituency we have a very large turkey industry at the present time although I would not say it is thriving because we do not have ample protection for poultry, especially turkeys. If the duty were sufficient to protect the turkey growers in Canada, it would expand into one of the great industries of this country, consuming much of the surplus grain that the prairies have at the present time.
In 1954, Canada imported over 5 million pounds of turkey from the United States; in 1955 she imported double that, or 10 million pounds. Now, what do we have in 1956? Up until February 11, the market report shows imports of 422,000 pounds, and for the same period in 1955 it was 96,000 pounds.

The official prediction from the United States department of agriculture is for an increase of 6 per cent in turkeys raised this year. With the Canadian tariff as it is, at 124 per cent ad valorem, if there were a break in the United States market owing to the tremendous amount of turkeys being raised this year the duty might well drop to three or four cents per pound.
I think that the turkey growers, of whom there are now a considerable number in Leeds county-and there will be more if they are adequately protected-are not asking for too much when they suggest that the tariff should be 12i per cent ad valorem, but not less than five cents per pound.
Under the present tariff, turkeys may come into Canada at a very low tariff when the price is lowest in the United States, and this may have a very damaging effect on our market here. The farmers are reasonable when they ask for protection only comparable to other industries in Canada. This they must have, if they are going to survive and play their part in expanding this country in the next fifty years, making it the great nation that we all visualize.
It is time the government woke up to the fact and admitted that all is not well with our basic industry. It is time it realized that there should be more equality in the distribution of our gross national income. Surely the government must realize that much of our present industrial prosperity can be attributed to credit buying. Without a very strong agricultural economy, I hesitate to imagine where this whole Canadian economy may drift.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on item No. 1 of the agriculture estimates and though I think my remarks will primarily be of interest to hon. members from the province of Ontario some of the topics which I discuss will no doubt be of interest to all the farmers in Canada.
The first suggestion I would like to make to the Minister of Agriculture would be that he broaden the broadcasts which occur at the luncheon and dinner hours regarding the marketing of livestock on the Toronto stock exchange. The reason for this is that the beef producers of Wellington county have sent a resolution to me asking not only that the price be given but that the number of beasts which are sold at that price be recorded. This would give the farmers some idea of the quantity of stock that is being handled and at what price that stock is being sold.
I feel there is great merit in this recommendation. I realize that these broadcasts are not paid for by our government but are handled as a news item, but I believe that the
67509-224J

department does furnish the various radio stations with this information.
The second point I have been asked to bring to the attention of the minister is that truckers are presently required to have their trucks disinfected after delivering stock to the stockyards. This requires that the trucks be washed. Many of the truckers buy cattle at the stockyards and on the return trip transport them back to the various farmers who require feeders. After they have been washed, the bottoms of the trucks are very slippery. Although I realize it is not the responsibility of the dominion government to look after the stockyards it might recommend to the provincial government that some sand be made available to the farmers which they could throw into the bottom of the trucks in order that they would not be slippery after the disinfecting process. Again this seems like a reasonable request to me, and I submit both problems to the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I shall be very glad to consider the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. I might immediately point out to him, however, that in the appointment of parliamentary assistants I understand that the assistant to a minister is so appointed to assist the minister of the crown in such manner and to such extent as the minister may determine, and to represent his department in the House of Commons in the absence of the minister. I make that comment immediately, but I shall be glad to take the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition under advisement.

Mr. Chairman, since you are taking it under advisement and have raised a question with regard to parliamentary assistants, I would point out that the presence of a parliamentary assistant has nothing to do with the point raised. Our system of the responsibility of the government implies the joint responsibility of all ministers and the capacity of a minister of the crown who is under a special oath in relation to that office to be able to speak on behalf of the whole government. That is where our system of government is clearly distinguished from that of the United States or from similar systems. Our system calls for the possibility of an answer by some minister capable of speaking on behalf of the government collectively.
The parliamentary assistant has certain duties and can speak in connection with certain limited matters on behalf of the minister to whom he has been appointed as assistant, but he is not sworn to the privy council and certainly is not in a position under any circumstances where he can speak with responsibility and authority on behalf of the government.

Mr. Chairman, I was in my office for a little while getting some information in case someone would ask some questions that had to do with what is before the committee at the present time. When I went out

the hon. member who was speaking was not dealing with my estimates at all and under the rules of this house he really should not have been allowed to continue.
There is nothing before the house at the moment as the house is in committee. I quite agree with the Leader of the Opposition when he says that when the house is sitting there should always be a minister present, and there should be a minister here while the house is in committee but not for the reason mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition.
There is only one thing under consideration, the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. The only questions which can be asked properly while the house is in committee on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture are questions related to those estimates. My assistant who is sitting beside me is quite capable of answering any question which any member of the opposition may be asking in the same manner as I would answer it, or perhaps in many respects much more effectively than I could do it.
I think there would be agreement on that.

There would be agreement that probably my hon. friend has more difficulty in putting up with the answers he gets from me than he would with the answers from most people, but that is the answer which the opposition is called upon to put up with. When the members of the opposition ask questions, they get answers which sometimes suit them and which sometimes do not. I want to assure the Leader of the Opposition that if he or any member of the official opposition has any question to ask about anything my assistant is quite capable of answering it.

Mr. Chairman, since the matter is under consideration and under advisement I would point out that the remarks of the right hon. minister have no bearing whatever on the point raised. I am quite sure that there would be many who would agree that there are a number of hon. members who are not sworn to the privy council who would be infinitely better in the position of Minister of Agriculture. But that is not the point. The point is that our system provides for the possibility of a question being asked at any time which may call for an answer from the government. Whoever the minister may be,
I submit that while the house is sitting with the Speaker in the chair, or in committee, a minister should be present and be in a position to speak on behalf of the government. I merely raised the point that no minister was present. We welcome the return of the Minister of Agriculture but that does not in any way change the point that I have raised.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since you are going to study the point may I ask you to give consideration to a couple of citations which may have a bearing on the matter. It seems to me that the Leader of the Opposition was perfectly right when he said that by custom at any rate there should always be a minister of the crown in the house. I think it is always accepted, as well as being laid down by the rules, that a committee of the house is an extension of the house and is governed by the same rules. The Minister of Agriculture cannot evade this question by saying that we are in committee rather than in the house.
It seems to me that the point made by the Leader of the Opposition is particularly true and carries particular force at the present time because we are dealing with the estimates. We have before us a resolution dealing with the expenditure of money. I would ask you to pay attention to section 54 of the British North America Act which has to do with the voting of money and which makes it clear that that can be done only at the instance of someone who can indicate to the house the recommendation of the Governor General. I would also draw your attention to citation 479 which reads:
Supply resolutions are submitted in the following terms: "Resolved that a sum not exceeding . be granted to His Majesty for . . . for the year ending 31st March, 194 ." Each resolution is moved by the minister for whose department the amount is to be voted.
Obviously under that citation we can only be discussing the estimate now before us if it is moved by a minister. It seems to me that it would follow that that minister should be here for the discussion on that estimate.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition, who has a home in my riding and whom I rather fancy I represent in the house, for causing a delay so the right hon. Minister of Agriculture could go to his office and be able to return to hear my remarks. However, I cannot allow the Leader of the Opposition to suggest that there is anyone in this house on either side who can do more for the farmers or who has done more for the farmers than the present Minister of Agriculture. The people of the whole of Canada know what a good fighter Jimmy Gardiner is. They admire him for it. They do not always agree with him, but no one can say that he has not fought for the farmer down through the years, in a way which has been a credit to those that he represents in agriculture.
If I might return to my discussion of a few points that I think are interesting to the farmers in our country, I should like to speak for just a moment about some observations that I made while I was in Europe. I took a trip abroad last summer during the recess to see and to learn about some of the conditions that exist in other countries, and I should like to pass on a comment or two on these, comparing them with the conditions in our own country.

Supply-Agriculture
The first I should like to mention has something to do with the fall fairs that our Department of Agriculture does a great deal to promote. There are larger fairs like the Royal Winter fair, and I was pleased to hear the address made by the Minister of Finance at the last Royal Winter fair, where he was prepared to listen to the requests of the governing body of that fair that they need a new addition to their coliseum. People who attend that fair know very well that the coliseum is inadequate, and it was very gratifying to listen to him take the lead in letting the people know that our Department of Agriculture appreciated this need and that it might, if conditions were right, be prepared to assist in seeing that an enlargement was carried out.
Turning to the use of this fair, I should like to discuss for a moment or two what I have seen abroad and how it compares with what we do here. I spent a week in Denmark and, thanks to our minister there, I was permitted to visit some of the hog feeding stations and to discuss how they have managed to raise those beautiful Landrace hogs.
I was informed that the farmers themselves felt that, if they were going to market their product, they had to produce a hog they could sell. One advantage that Denmark has over us is that it has a good market for sow belly, the type of meat that we find difficult to handle and get rid of in this country. The German market is close to Denmark, and is a very good market for what is more or less a waste part of the pig in Canada.
They had to do two things. They had to capture the British market, and therefore they had to produce good bacon. There came a time when they had to get United States dollars, and the only source of United States dollars that they had in that country was for hams, and so they had to produce a pig that had good hams as well as good bacon in order to get United States dollars. The farmers of that country decided that they would set up stations that would feed test hogs so that they would produce the best type of hog for bacon and ham. Three or four years ago, before they needed the United States dollars, they produced a hog with a Wiltshire side of some 36 inches in length. For the benefit of hon. members I might say that we produce in Canada a grade A hog, one that has a side of 29 inches. A good hog in Canada has a side 32 inches long.
They have been encouraged to breed this type of hog because fairs and shows in that country will give prizes to hogs only on their performance. They do not give prizes to hogs on appearance. Let me ask the minister to speak to the judges, if he thinks it is wise, in regard to changing the method of

judging hogs in Canada. In Denmark a hog to get first prize, has to be the type of beast that will cut up and make good Wiltshire sides with good hams.
Let me quote a few figures. At the Toronto show we had some hogs exhibited by Prince Edward Island, in the Todd trophy class. Prince Edward Island had 16 exhibits and won 13 prizes. This class is judged on the carcasses, so that the judges can view the ham and the bacon side. With regard to the Brethour trophy we had a similar situation where the hogs from Prince Edward Island entered in some 15 classes won, I believe, 12 prizes. Yet in the live classes similar pigs from the island did not get one first-class award. So I would ask the minister, considering the donations we make to these fairs, whether it would not be wise to ask the judges whether it would not be better to give prizes to live hogs for the type of hog that when killed will give us good bacon and good ham.
I also learned some other things when I was in Denmark. The Danish farmers told me that they had to buy our feed grain, ship it from Canada to Denmark, feed it and then send the dead carcasses back to England in competition with our pork. I asked them how they managed to do this. They said, "Well, there are two or three things that we do a little differently from you people. One is that we must feed carefully. We cannot feed our hogs in a wasteful manner. We have learned that it takes two pounds of feed to put a pound of pork on a pig that weighs 50 pounds. It takes five pounds of feed to put a pound of pork on a pig that weighs 200 pounds." So, if we are going to be efficient, we must ship out lighter weight grade A hogs.
At this point I should like to commend the minister for the stand that he has always taken in supporting our farmers when they produce grade A hogs. It is very important that we continue this bonus even when other governments have seen fit to withdraw their donations for grade A hogs. I should like to recommend that we double our payment to $4 on grade A hogs-that would give an extra $2-in order to encourage the farmers to proceed along the route on which they have now started in Canada. They realize, and with good sense, that we have to produce a type of bacon which the Americans like. We are able to sell our hogs now in the United States market and get 4 to 5 cents more than the Americans can get for their fat-fed hogs. Our farmers have done a good job at working to produce grade A hogs, and this would be a tremendous encouragement for them to continue to do that. I would not want to take credit for suggesting this for the first time,

because four years ago Mr. Arnold Darroch, the member at that time for Wellington North, recommended this program.
Since I have been abroad and have seen what can be done with careful feeding, and with fairs that are judged on producing a product which when killed is what is desired rather than for it's good looks when it is alive, and by seeing the type of Danish pig that has taken away from Canada our market in Great Britain, I think it is well that we make moves to assist our farmers to produce a similar pig here. I believe that next year the method of buying by the British government will end and that the private buyers of Great Britain will be coming to Canada and looking for their own goods. Farm products will not be bought by the government any more. If we have the type of pork the British want, and I am now referring to side bacon, we will have a chance to recapture the market that has been lost to us for the past three years. At least we will be competitive, and we will be able to be proud of what we have done.
When I was in the United States a year ago I discovered that the Americans were selling a Canadian type of bacon there, a product which they were advertising very strongly. This suggests the Americans envy the program of producing leaner bacon which your department has encouraged and to which the farmers have co-operated so well. If we encourage our farmers to be a little more efficient in feeding their pigs and to sell them before they get too heavy so that they do not eat too much and put on that last few pounds, we will not have hogs with 30 to 40 pounds of fat. A grade A hog generally turns out to have about 20 pounds of fat on the carcass which cannot be sold as pork. A grade B hog has about 30 pounds of fat and a grade C hog about 45 pounds of fat. It is generally in the last stage of feeding pigs, in what might be termed the inefficient stage, that the fat is put on. All of these suggestions that I make hinge on the production of more grade A hogs in the hogs that are raised.
Coming back again to the question of the fairs or shows that we have, in Scotland and northern England a wonderful market has been created for show cattle. I think most people agree that the British Isles have brought about a wonderful market for show cattle. They have gone to great pains to create that market, but I do not think many people in Canada feel that this type of show beasts we buy from these markets are good cattle to put in our barns and pens and feed to be killed for beef. There are not many people who want to buy the beef that comes from these show beasts and use it in their homes. There is a perfectly good reason for that. It is much too fat.

However, Great Britain is a small country and they have produced this type of beast because it catches the fancy of the wealthy American and Canadian show buyer, and we have followed suit in judging our show beasts. I do not think there is anything that has been more harmful with respect to the type of cattle we wish to market than the type of show beast that we have raised in this country. Exactly the same thing is true of hogs. We have not paid enough attention to the carcasses of these show beasts and what we get out of them when they are killed.
There is one more thing we do that I should like the minister to look into. When we kill a grade A pig we measure three fingers from the H bone at the hip, cut it off there, and that is considered the ham. We go to the third rib from the front shoulder, we cut it off at the centre of the third rib, we then have a side and a shoulder. If we follow that plan in cutting the shoulders with regard to the long Danish hogs that are 36 inches in length we have a front shoulder weighing somewhere about 44 pounds. The reason for that is that the Danish pig has been bred in such a way that each vertebra takes up more room and by cutting at the third rib on a long pig you have added a lot of extra shoulder.
The Danes have got away from that. They measure three fingers from the first rib and cut it off there in the same way as is done in the case of the rear quarter. On a long-vertebrae pig, that may mean cutting it at the second rib. So they get about four pounds extra of good side bacon. We should look into that situation. I think a committee could well be set up to look into the matter of supplying information to the farmers with regard to producing the best beasts and the actual amount of profitable meat they get out of them.
I would hope that these matters would receive some consideration during the next year. I should like to mention one other thing that is troublesome to our farmers, the price of butter, the price of cheese and the price of powdered milk. I would ask the minister to look very carefully at the situation with respect to cheese and powdered milk: I believe that in the opinion of most people the minister has done an excellent job with his butter program, but I would not want anyone to think I was recommending the same treatment for cheese and powdered milk. There might be some other way that this problem could be handled.

I would ask the minister to look at that matter carefully and see what he can do.
