Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the minister's estimates I propose to deal with one specific problem which is related to agriculture in all Canada. My colleagues have dealt and will deal with other aspects of agriculture in our Canadian economy outlining the decline in our share of the national income and making suggestions which we would like to see adopted to improve the welfare of agriculture. I am pleased to note that the hon. member for Wellington South has been listening to some of the speeches made by members of this group and that he too advocates an increase in the premium on grade A hogs. That is a view that has been voiced by members of this group.
The hon. member said that he had had the opportunity of visiting Denmark but I wish that he had travelled a little more throughout the countryside of Ontario so that he would have a better appreciation of agriculture. I noticed that, particularly when he used terms such as "dead carcass". Personally I have never seen a live carcass. I was wondering where he got his terminology.
He also took the opportunity to express his congratulations to the Minister of Agriculture and I noticed that the hon. member for Leeds was quite envious of the fact that the minister represents western Canada. If a poll were to be conducted among the farmers of western Canada I think you would find they would be only too pleased to give the hon. member the present Minister of Agriculture so that the people of Ontario could have him.
The problem I wish to deal with specifically is a very important one and it can only be brought up at this stage because it concerns several items of the minister's estimates. It is related to the present congested condition we have on western farms and perhaps that is one reason why the government has not been too active in trying to solve the problem. I wish to deal more specifically with the tremendous inroads that weeds have made on the agricultural economy. This is particularly important now because of the decline of agriculture's share of the country's income. The farmers do not have the finances with which to carry out proper cultural practices to eradicate the weeds that are making such inroads. The matter is of direct concern to farmers in all parts of Canada because many of the cultivating operations that they perform are directly aimed at eradicating weeds so that the crops they plant will be able to benefit from the available moisture. The municipalities in all parts of Canada-including

your counties in Ontario-are familiar with the problem of weeds along country roads and in the fields. I think we should make a brief survey of the magnitude of this problem in relation to the Canadian economy. Mr. H. E. Wood, chairman of the Manitoba weeds commission in 1953 pointed out this, and I will quote from the Manitoba Cooperator of June 30, 1955:
Mr. Wood said he had undertaken an estimate of the toll weeds extracted from prairie agriculture. On the basis of the 1953 crop, the cost of weeds amounted to $255 million, or for the 248,000 farms, an average of $1,028 per farm.
That is one of the factors which is certainly drawing down the agriculturalist's share of the national income. It has been estimated that wild oats are a direct cost of over $500 per farm. I think the minister is aware of conditions which exist in his own area and which are prevalent in my area where farmers are forced to go out and cut out acres of badly infested sloughs in order to prevent the reseeding of the wild oats. There are areas which have been virtually taken out of cultivation because of infestation by this weed.
Mr. A. H. Martin, director of the crops, seeds and weeds branch in Ontario, has estimated that weed losses in that province are $4.65 an acre or approximately 14 per cent of the field crop value.
It has been estimated that the over-all cost of weeds far exceeds the combined losses due to insects and disease. I think we can appreciate the magnitude of that problem when statements such as that are made by people in responsible positions. The individual farmer, of course, is very much aware of the impact of weeds on his agricultural production. When chemical weed controls were first introduced we found the farmers receptive to their use. In the early years of chemical weed control we were advised not to use 2,4-D on flax. The farmers were so far ahead of scientific research that they found that, by reducing the application, 2,4-D was extremely effective for use on flax.
The municipalities are closely associated with this problem. I have a letter from Tramping Lake, Saskatchewan, written by Mr. Ralph Fluney, councillor for division 2 of rural municipality No. 380. He writes as follows:
This municipality 380 spends about $2,000 each year trying to kill this weed. Other R.M.'s adjoining ours spend more and in and around Marsden they have gone broke trying to kill this weed. I have some patches on my own land and know what I am talking about.
The debate which we had in the early part of this week ties in closely with this problem that the councillor for the rural municipality of Tramping Lake points out,

namely that the Anal responsibility is apparently resting on the shoulders of the municipal authorities. They have the responsibility for appointing weed inspectors and for acquiring and utilizing chemical weed controls through high-pressure sprayers so that these weeds which are showing up in the municipality and which are a threat to the welfare of the individual farmers in that municipality can be controlled. It also is the responsibility of rural municipalities-and they are accepting it-to build municipal seed cleaning plants, something which of course puts another direct cost on the farmers, and hence on the municipal authorities.
I think we should make a study into the infestation of noxious weeds in the various parts of Canada so that we would be in a position to suggest to the science service and to the experimental farm service what action they can take to deal with these problems. The worst weeds that we have in Saskatchewan at the moment are toadflax, Russian knapweed, hoary cress and leafy spurge. Toadflax is one that is very prevalent in certain areas of the province. Toadflax called linaria vulgaris was found in North America as early as 1758. The first specimen was collected in the University of Saskatchewan herbarium in 1918. The weed survey in 1955 states:
This species was found to infest 134,602 acres in 4,583 quarter-sections in 78 municipalities within the surveyed area.
It has established itself since 1918 to cover nearly 150,000 acres. A resurvey was made in 1955 and the results of that resurvey are frightening:
In R.M. No. 372 the number of acres infested increased from 114 to 311 from 1952 to 1954, while the number of infested quarters increased from 83 to 108 .. .
In R.M. No. 440 the number of patches increased from 2,650 to 9,869 from 1949 to 1953, while the number of infested quarter-sections increased from 607 to 729.
That gives us some idea of the inroads that this weed is making in the agricultural economy, because once your land becomes infested with toadflax, virtually nothing can be done about it with the present knowledge we have. The agricultural representative service in the province of Saskatchewan is providing an invaluable service in organizing a front-line attack against these weeds. They are working closely with the agricultural committees of the rural municipalities to discover and to control patches. In fact, the agricultural committee of my own municipality, R.M. No. 290, informed me that Macedonian toadflax was being advertised for sale in an eastern seed house. I recall asking a question of the Minister of Agriculture on February 22, 1955.
Supply-Agriculture
I asked the minister whether he had taken action to control the sale of Macedonian toadflax by this seed house. The minister replied in part:
In reply I wish to state that the control of weeds is a provincial and municipal responsibility.
Farther on he stated:
There is no legislation that forbids a seed house selling a plant such as Macedonian toadflax. It is an ornamental flower.
That answer, Mr. Chairman, showed that the Minister of Agriculture was still farming with horses, that he was miles behind the times because the regulations concerning seeds were changed to allow better control of linaria vulgaris, linaria dalmatica and linaria macedonica. In fact, the Canada Gazette of November 10, 1954, lists all the species of toadflax as being a primary noxious weed. The minister knows that if it is a primary noxious weed, no seeds are allowed in registered certified or No. 1 seed. I think we must broaden our thinking on this whole approach to weeds. The horse-farming technique is not good enough when you are dealing with a problem that is moving so rapidly. The weed survey in 1955 had this to say on broad-leaved toadflax. It is interesting enough to quote:
Within the past decade a broad-leaved species of toadflax, linaria dalmatica, has become troublesome as a persistent perennial weed in parts of Washington and Idaho. This species is the same as one which is spreading in Saskatchewan. Seventy-nine small infestations of this species have been found within the surveyed area. Many of these occur in gardens and cemeteries. Undoubtedly many more infestations occur, since the field men were not asked to note these infestations until the 1953 survey.
The minister may argue that linaria dalmatica and linaria macedonica are two different varieties when in fact they are, according to the authorities whom I have consulted in the University of Saskatchewan, a strain of the same species. I was most disappointed with the attitude that the minister took on this problem. Nevertheless, even though the minister did make that mistake at that time, he might be prepared to admit it and to follow some of the suggestions I am going to make now so that the matter of weeds can be more effectively controlled in the future.
On many occasions the Liberal party has hidden under the skirts of the British North America Act. In this case they cannot evade their responsibility because agricultural research is explicitly outlined as a federal responsibility. What is being done in connection with research on this whole matter of weed control? Last year I put a question on the order paper and received as an order for return sessional paper No. 213 which gave

Supply-Agriculture
information as to what was spent on weed control as opposed to another important aspect of agriculture, namely, entomology. I found that in 1954 there were eight full-time weed control specialists in the whole dominion of Canada. Six of them were located at headquarters at Ottawa, one in Ontario and one in Alberta. The total amount of money spent in salaries of these individuals was $37,055. When you compare that with entomology you find that there were 256 employed as full-time entomologists at an expense of $1,176,977. I am not saying that we should reduce the amount of money that is spent on entomological research but I am saying we should certainly pay more attention to the agricultural research that should be done in connection with weeds.
Dr. R. O. Ripley, chairman of the national weed committee, has estimated that in 1953 the total cost of weed investigation at the dominion and university level was $110,658. We find that outside of the Ottawa headquarters science service and experimental farm services there are no botanists working on this problem of weed control. We should take immediate steps to establish a chain of laboratories to investigate the problem. We should establish a D.E.W. line against weeds. This same suggestion might involve another change that I feel should be made in departmental administration. For some time now I have felt that there is a duplication of services in the science service and in the experimental farm service. I feel that in many instances the headquarters are located in identical stations. For example, there is a science service and an experimental station at Lethbridge. The same thing is true at Kentville, Nova Scotia. There would certainly be increased efficiency if the experimental farm service and the science service were amalgamated so that the professional men working in entomology and the field men working in experimental farm service could correlate their activities.
In connection with this same weed problem, we find that an investigation was carried on at the Belleville parasite laboratories where, incidentally, they employ 40 entomologists who are trying to find parasites which control weeds. One of them found a parasite on the toadflax samples which were sent down from Saskatchewan which seemed to do considerable damage to the reproductive mechanism of the toadflax. They found two insects on toadflax samples in Ontario where toadflax is not a serious weed. I would suppose that with the seriousness of this weed in western Canada the authorities in the science service would have immediately established a regional laboratory in the Marsden area fMr. Johnson (Kindersley).]
where this insect could be controlled to see if it would effectively control toadflax, but nothing was done. In fact, one part-time man at the Scott experimental station has been moved to Lethbridge so that there is no one there except those who are on loan from the field husbandry department.
I do not think it is a matter of pleading with the minister to take action on this particular problem; I do not think he ever thought of it before. But if we are to be serious in our approach to weeds which are, as I mentioned, so expensive to farmers in all parts of Canada, something must be done immediately to stem the tide because it is far better to do it now than even five years from now when there might be from 500,000 to 1 million acres seriously infected. The onus of responsibility is on the federal government. The farmers in all parts of Canada feel that it is the responsibility of the federal government to perform this useful function, and although it might be contrary to Liberal policy, they might increase the surplus of wheat which we have for future generations to benefit thereby.

I would like to take six or seven minutes this afternoon to discuss one specific subject, namely, the lack of adequate long-term credit in agriculture throughout the country. As a matter of fact, I think hon. members on both sides of the house would agree that many of the difficulties which farmers have today can be traced to the lack of such facilities. At the present time, almost every branch of agriculture is suffering because they are starved for working capital.
The reason for this undesirable situation is not difficult to find. Apparently, private capital is failing to meet the problem posed by the lack of farm credit. Today private lenders, whether they are banks, investment houses or mortgage companies, can find more lucrative fields in which to invest their money, and fields which are less risky. As a result, in latter years these companies have been placing an ever smaller amount of their investment funds in farm mortgages.
I think the Bank of Canada regulations curtailing credit, which we have recently seen, will make this situation worse. The squeeze on farmers is bound to become even more serious. I can understand the lack of enthusiasm, which lending companies have; yet, I would like to tell them that their neglect of the long-term farm credit field could have serious consequences, not only to the nation but also to themselves. If the private lending companies do not devise methods whereby farmers can get adequate long-term credit, the government will have to come into the field in an ever more extensive way.

I am going to suggest today that these lending companies, if they are to take the advantages of the free enterprise system, should also assume some of the responsibilities. One of the responsibilities should be the granting of better long-term credit to farmers.
The lack of adequate credit today is having serious effects on our farming communities. In the first place, many young farmers who would like to go into farming are moving into the towns and cities, because they cannot get sufficient money to go into farming. After all, the price of land has skyrocketed and the price of machinery is very high. Moreover it is difficult for young farmers to find sufficient money to purchase a basic herd. Thus many young farmers who cannot obtain adequate credit are leaving the rural areas.
In the second place I suggest that a lack of adequate farm credit today is causing a concentration of farms in the hands of fewer and fewer farmers, because such credit as is available invariably goes to the wealthier farmers. This means inevitably that the number of marginal farmers tends to decrease while the number of tenant farmers tends to increase. I suggest that adequate farm credit could reverse such a trend.
I would like to point out in the third place that adequate farm credit today is lowering the productivity of many Canadian farmers. Farming is like most other businesses, in that the old adage that "it takes money to make money" is just as true as elsewhere. If our farmers could get better credit today, I think they would go into extensive irrigation projects, reclamation works, regrassing, etc. They would purchase better livestock and so on.
The farm credit problem is resulting in a lower productivity on farms than is necessary. Thus I suggest that parliament should give the problem attention without delay.
The government has recognized the problem this session with two amendments, one to the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the other to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. Both of these amendments are welcome; yet I think most hon. members would agree that all they can do is nibble at an over-all solution. As in the past, I am still convinced that farmers who go to make loans under the provisions of those acts will find that the down payments required are too high, the security requirements are too severe, or the actual amount which can be borrowed is too small.
I point these facts out because under those acts only about 15 per cent of all farm loans are made. We have to take additional action if the situation is to be solved.
Supply-Agriculture
It seems to me that the real answer to this long-term farm credit problem is not to oe found in direct government loans. I think a method must be found to encourage private Canadian lending institutions to re-enter and greatly expand their activities in the farm mortgage business. I have a suggestion as to how this could be accomplished.
As I said a moment ago, many of our lending institutions feel-and I must admit perhaps with some justification-that marginal farmers are too great a risk because of climatic conditions, because of the uncertainties of markets and prices, et cetera to be given 20 year loans. As a result the farmers who really need money today very frequently cannot get it.
I remind hon. members of this house that the banks and lending institutions took the same attitude a few years ago toward urban dwellers who wanted to borrow money for a 20 or 30-year period to build a house. Parliament rectified that situation very successfully about three years ago, when it introduced legislation which guaranteed the banks against losses on 20 or 30 year loans made to urban dwellers to build homes.
I suggest that it would be feasible today to give the banks a similar guarantee on losses which they might incur by making 20 or 25 year loans to farmers to buy new farms or to buy equipment. In other words, I think parliament should consider having a national farm credit act along the lines of the National Housing Act.
As I see it, the principle would be precisely the same in both cases. Under that legislation the farmers would be able to get long-term farm credit without an unbearable burden being put on the taxpayers. Since the banks are making long-term loans under the National Housing Act, I think they might also be prepared to give the farmers longterm credit if suitable guarantees against losses were given by parliament.
I repeat that the time has come for the house to come to grips with this problem. Canadian agriculture must have better longterm credit facilities. In a booming economy we cannot permit agriculture to lag so far behind other industries.

Mr. Chairman, the house will recall that on July 22 last year I spoke on the estimates for agriculture and made a request for a dominion experimental station in Norfolk. I do not intend to make the same speech all over again but there are a few points I would like to re-emphasize.
First of all, farm income has not risen with other lines of endeavour and in some cases it has declined. This would be bad

Supply-Agriculture
in any event, but to make matters worse our operating costs have risen sharply and farmers are now in a squeeze that could be disastrous if nothing is done about it.
One way for government assistance to work to the advantage of our farmers would be for us to have this experimental farm located in Norfolk so that farmers could, under direction, work out some of our problems. I think perhaps our needs are greater now than they were in 1955 and I am renewing the request for this station.
Our temperature in Norfolk is about five degrees lower than at Harrow and Vineland, the other two government stations, and varieties that do well there would not give us the same production under our different growing conditions and temperatures.
My request of last year has won universal support in Norfolk and it has particularly won the support of the county council which sent four of its members here on April 24 to support the request for a station.
Bruce Wallace, who is a large apple and cherry grower and manager of Norfolk Fruit Growers and Norfolk Berry Growers, met the minister with us. We were favourably received by the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance and the deputy minister of agriculture.
The press in Norfolk has also supported the request both editorially and in news items. The London Free Press and the Brantford Expositor have also given the request much support.
I think perhaps the committee will bear with me if I quote some of the production figures I gave last year. I regret that these figures are for the year 1954 and perhaps are not quite relevant to the year which has passed.
First of all, we had 2,000 acres of apples in Norfolk and 400,000 bushels were produced in 1954. Last year we had relatively the same acreage but we produced many more apples and experienced some difficulty in selling them. There were 30 acres of sweet cherries and we produced 640 bushels. There were 142 acres of sour cherries and we produced 16,730 bushels. That was in 1954, Mr. Chairman. In 1955 sour cherries were about double and again we experienced some trouble in disposing of them.
There were 500 acres of peaches which produced over 60,000 bushels. There were 66 acres of Bartlett pears which produced 20,000 bushels. There were 103 acres of Keifer pears which produced 16,000 bushels. Now I would like to deal with strawberries.
Would the hon. member speak up a little more.

We had 1,100 acres of strawberries in 1954 which produced 3,300,000 quarts and in 1955 this production was well over 4 millions quarts. Our production has increased a little in the two years. We expect we will have a very heavy crop in 1956 because they weathered the winter well.
I wish now to deal with fresh market vegetables. We had a production of 15,000 bushels of tomatoes and 175,000 bushels of potatoes in 1954 and last year it was about the same.
Would my hon. friend tell us what section he is speaking about when he says "we"? I am sorry but I did not hear his introductory remarks.

I am speaking mainly for
the people of the county of Norfolk and the counties surrounding Norfolk.
In the area between Simcoe and Port Dover there was produced in 1954 a total of 450,000 crates of sweet corn. Some of that was exported after being precooled. More of this crop could be grown.
Something else that is new in Norfolk is irrigation. The tobacco men have miles and miles of irrigation pipe. They use the creeks as a water supply and also any low-lying areas which fill up in the winter with water which can be used when needed. This provides a problem because we are not too sure yet as to what we are doing. Sometimes too much irrigation will ruin a crop and it must be applied at the right time. There is an old saying that every farmer has a stiff neck because he is always watching the sun and the clouds. Weather determines what we are going to do from day to day.
We need new varieties, especially in strawberries. Twenty years ago we had a variety called the Parson Beauty that produced quite well for years. Lately the Premier variety has predominated but we are always looking for a new variety which will produce well and remain firm in shipping.
There is an experimental tobacco station at Delhi, but the soil there is not representative of the county. It will grow tobacco but not all kinds of fruits and vegetables. Perhaps the minister could see his way clear to allowing the office there to be used so that any directions could go out from that point. I would respectfully request that the minister give careful consideration to this matter in the light of the support that has been forthcoming from every part of the farm population of Norfolk and in view of our increasing need.
I should like also to support the hon. member for Wellington South in his request that the premium on grade A hogs be increased

and that the premium on grade B hogs remain the same. This would tend to add quality to our bacon and assist in our exports.

Mr. Chairman, it gives me great pleasure to take part in this debate, particularly when we are discussing the estimates of the one department which is of great concern to a large majority of my constituents.
During my trip home at the Easter recess it was my privilege to attend the graduation exercises at the Vermilion school of agriculture. I know that the Department of Agriculture does not make any grants toward the operation of schools of agriculture in Alberta, but another department does make grants to the three schools we have. The total grants from the federal treasury to the province of Alberta in this connection I believe is in the neighbourhood of $47,700. There are three such schools in the province, one at Olds, another at Fairview and another at Vermilion in my constituency.
These schools give a very practical type of education to the young farmers and homemakers of the province. However, there is one disturbing factor about the operation of these schools, in that attendance is gradually decreasing. Does that mean that the young people of western Canada have lost faith in the future of the agricultural industry? It may just happen that that is the case. If it is the case, then I feel that all governments should view the situation with alarm.
It has been pointed out time and time again during this session that net farm income has been steadily decreasing during the last number of years. For example, in 1952 it was down 3 [DOT] 13 per cent of what it was the previous year; in 1953 it was down 21-6 per cent; and in 1954 it was down 66-64 per cent. This disastrous trend must be halted if we are going to maintain any semblance of development in Canada's major industry. I submit that Canadian citizens are justified in looking to the senior government for some direction and action in this regard.
During the graduation exercises which I attended at the Vermilion school they held what is known as the Little Royal, which is fashioned after the Royal Winter Fair at Toronto. I was interested in following their program. They put on a splendid stock show where the young students were able to demonstrate their training in such things as the judging of stock and showmanship. As I went through the plant I saw displayed the work of the carpentry shop, the welding shop and the meat-cutting department. I was quite interested in a remark made this afternoon by an hon. member who was telling how it was
Supply-Agriculture
possible to get a larger sized side of bacon from a dead carcass. I have yet to see a living carcass.
Continuing through the school we saw the dairying plant and then we went into the portion of the school used by the homemakers where cooking, dressmaking and so on were taught. This is good practical training as far as the young people of our province are concerned. We should be encouraging young people to take greater advantage of this type of training. Agriculture in our province as in other parts of Canada indicates that the average age of farmers actively engaged is rapidly going up.
I feel that in order to be successful a farmer must be trained, that the proper training is more important than perhaps even a healthy body. The day of the strong back and the farmer going together in order to make a success is long past.
I should like to congratulate the federal government upon the grants being made for this type of education. I would ask the federal government to take immediate steps to do something toward stabilizing the agricultural industry. If that were done I do not think any other incentive would be needed to get our young people to stay on the farm.
During the present session we have discussed at some length resolutions extending the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Canadian Farm Loan Act. These acts are good as far as they go and the machinery which is to be provided is better than before. However, I would point out that the machinery will be no good unless the policy of the government expressed through these boards is changed and the conservative elements found on the boards during the past few years removed so that these two acts may serve the purpose which we as members of parliament trust they will.
There is another matter I should like to bring briefly to the attention of the minister, and that is the ever-increasing cost of commercial fertilizers to the farmers of the west. This morning I was reading a report issued by the Department of Agriculture which stated that the cost of commercial fertilizers had not gone up last year, and that it was hoped the upward trend had been halted. However, I should like to submit that the rise in the cost of fertilizers over the past years has been far too great. I hold in my hand some delivery slips given to farmers at the time they purchased fertilizers throughout the years. All these will deal with the cost of ammonium phosphate 11-48-0.
On June 21, 1946, you could buy a ton of this fertilizer for $58.50. By April 2, 1949, the same type of fertilizer had gone up to

Supply-Agriculture
$74.40 per ton. By November 8, 1950, the farmer was forced to pay $85.35 per ton. By April 15, 1952, it was $97.70 per ton. On May 29, 1952, the farmer was charged $100.15 per ton. In the fall of that year it was $105.60. Last summer, on May 10, 1955, the price was up to $107.
I have tried to get some information as to why these prices have risen so sharply over the years. I am given to understand there are only two large plants producing commercial fertilizers in Canada, and I am wondering whether those two plants are not exercising some sort of monopolistic control over prices. If that is the case, I submit the Minister of Agriculture would be well advised to take a very close look at the situation and try to do something about it.
I just want to point out that in the course of a few years fertilizers which we wish the farmers of western Canada to use, and which they must use if they are to retain the fertility of their soil, have more than doubled in price.
Now I should like to spend a few moments discussing the hog industry as it affects the province of Alberta, and particularly as it affects the producers of hogs in my area. During the first half of 1954 hogs were sold at $33.33 per hundredweight. During the second half of that year they were sold at $24.92 per hundredweight. During the first half of 1955 they were $23.52 per hundredweight, and in the second half of 1955 $23.17 per hundredweight. I have taken these statistics from the Livestock Marketing Review. They point out that hog prices have dropped 33J per cent in the last two years. This is serious, because in our province we produce nearly one and a half million hogs a year.
I should like to point out that the livestock report in the Edmonton Journal of April 14, 1956, has this to say concerning hogs:
Hog prices dropped 50 cents at Winnipeg to 20-23 and Montreal was unchanged at 23-23-50. Toronto hog prices declined 50 cents to 23 and most Saskatchewan markets were down the same at 19. Prices remained steady at Vancouver at 22-15 for top grade hogs.
, In my constituency I have several large hog producers, and one of these producers has had extensive correspondence with the Minister of Agriculture in the past few months. This gentleman is a young man who is interested in the hog industry, has been in it for years and is hoping to make it his lifework, but if the present trend continues he will likely have to do what it has been suggested that he do,' quit raising hogs. However, he wrote the Minister of Agriculture in December,- 1955. I shall just take one
rMr. Smith (Battle River-Camrose) .1
paragraph of his letter. The minister has the letter and knows it is true:
I can't make enough money out of hogs after paying expenses and raising my family to pay my debts. The only reason I continue on is to live in hopes that your government will do something; that will give we farmers parity prices. Our prices have dropped but the prices we pay haven't come down.
I think he has summarized the situation fairly well as far as the hog producers are concerned. Perhaps it may be argued that, after all, hogs are only a sideline as far as the majority of the farmers in the west are concerned, though I do not accept that argument. I say that the hog industry in Alberta is one of the major branches of agriculture in our province. Last year, for example, we produced 1,691,193 hogs in the province of Alberta. That is not a small-time-business.
For that reason I should like to put on the record this afternoon a few figures I have been fortunate enough to secure. These figures are based on an actual 42-sow unit operated for the purpose of producing weaner pigs, and follow the project right from the time the pigs are born to the time they are marketed. It is pointed out that the following figures represent the cost to produce a hog:
Assuming that feed mixture consists of one-third oats and two-thirds barley, with 200 pounds, of concentrate in one ton of feed, the cost per cwt. is . . . $2.15.
That is the cost of feed for pigs. I do not wish to burden the committee with a lot of figures. Perhaps I shall put the others on record another time, but I want to point out that the cost of a 30-pound weaner pig has been estimated at $9.17. They give the cost of raising this 30-pound pig to 200 pounds. The cost of feed is $16.45. The cost of straw for bedding is 78 cents. The cost of incidentals and overhead, etc., is $1. Labour costs and weaning to market cost $3.50 per head. Marketing cost is $1. The total cost per pig, according to this survey, is $31.90 for this group of hogs. That is what it actually costs the producers to raise these hogs.
Assuming that 40 per cent of these hogs are graded A, 54 per cent B-l and 6 per cent C, and also assuming that the prices received for grade A hogs on the markets of the west are $20 per.hundredweight-and that is very generous now, by the way-grade B-l $19 per hundredweight and grade C $16.50 per hundredweight, what happens? There would be sold 254 grade A hogs from this 42-sow unit; there would be 343 hogs grade B-l and 38 hogs grade C. The average sale price of this group of fiogs which started out iri the weaner stage would be $30.60. To the producer the net loss per hog Would be $1.30.

Surely the minister will agree with me that a hog raiser who is going into it in a scientific manner cannot continue too long when he is losing $1.30 per hog. The minister will perhaps be able to advance other figures as to how much it costs to raise a hog. If he has them I would certainly appreciate it if he would put them on the record so we can look at them.
I have already pointed out that according to the figures of the federal government, during the course of 1955 there were 1,691,193 hogs raised in Alberta exclusive of domestic slaughterings and so on. What happened to those hogs? One-third were consumed right in the province of Alberta, and I am given to understand that 90 per cent of the remainder were shipped live weight or dressed to the Vancouver market. That being the case, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture how he can justify a support price for hogs of $18.50 on the Edmonton market and $23 on the Toronto and Montreal markets. When we consider the fact that the actual selling price of hogs on the Edmonton market is not much above the support price of $18.50 and that it costs $1 per hundredweight to ship those that are sent to the Vancouver markets, making $19.50, surely the farmers of Alberta are being given a bad time by a deal like this.
Somebody is making a huge profit out of the hogs that are raised in the province of Alberta, and I have already pointed out that it is not the producer. Somewhere along the line somebody is making money which rightfully belongs to the farmers of the province of Alberta. I submit to the minister that he should give very serious consideration to the establishment of a uniform floor price on hogs across Canada. I can see no reason that would justify the minister in establishing a floor price of $23 in Toronto and Montreal and $18.50 in Edmonton. It is nothing but straight discrimination against the hog producers of the province of Alberta. I will undoubtedly have the privilege of receiving a reply from the minister in this regard, and I am sure there will be many interesting discussions with respect to the hog industry.
I should like to say one thing more. I got into a little trouble the other day when I congratulated a civil servant. I do not wish to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture, but I should like to say to him that I have enjoyed the courtesy which members of his department have extended to me during my time here.

Mr. Chairman, when the Minister of Agriculture opened the discussion on his estimates a couple of months ago now I listened with a great deal of interest and
Supply-Agriculture
since then I have read what he had to say in Hansard. I must say that much of his speech was very interesting but that parts of it reminded me of a story that is told about a clergyman who on one occasion lost the notes for his sermon. They were picked up by a very curious member of his flock, who looked at the notes and was amazed to see a notation on the side which said, "Argument weak here; shout." I do not suggest that the minister-shouts but on reading his speech I came to the conclusion that it would be very apt if one were to put the notation beside certain portions of his speech, "Argument weak here; use some statistics."
Of course I am not criticizing the minister for doing that because it is quite a legitimate practice; nevertheless those who are on the receiving end of speeches that quote statistics at considerable length should be on their guard. In that connection I came across an interesting passage regarding statistics in a very famous book, "Mathematics for the-Millions". This book was written by a Mr. Hogben and he has this to say:
Today the lives and happiness of people depend more than most of us realize upon the correct interpretation of public statistics which are kept by government offices. When a committee of experts announce that the average man can live on his unemployment allowance, or the average child is getting sufficient milk, the mere mention of an average or the citation of a list of figures is enough to paralyse intelligent criticism. In reality half or more than half the population may not be getting enough to live on when the average man or child has enough. The majority of people living today in civilized countries cannot read and write freely in statistics. The modern man has got to learn the language of statistics in selfdefence, because no society is safe in the hands of its clever people.
In that regard I should like to make a few brief observations on some of the statistics the minister gave. He put tables on the record indicating farm cash income over a period of years and also farm net income for a number of years. These are very interesting figures. They show that, although generally speaking gross farm income is rising, over the last few years there has been a fairly rapid decline in net income. I refer only to the maritime provinces. In 1951 net farm income for the maritimes was, in round figures, $81 million, in 1952, $77 million, in.
1953,	$62 million and $62 million again in
1954.
Then there is another element in these income figures which should be realized, namely that they are not measured in constant dollars. Therefore although the farmer's net income may remain stationary or even increase, his purchasing power may be going down. That has been the case over the last few years. For example, in 1954 the percentage of the

Supply-Agriculture
gross national product which was credited to farm net income was 6-8, whereas the average for 1946 to 1950 inclusive was 12-7 per cent. The percentage of 6-8 for 1954 is the lowest percentage since 1931.
I think the minister is perfectly sincere. After all, it is his job to try to examine objectively, if possible, the true situation as far as the agricultural industry of our country is concerned. But I am rather disappointed by the fact that due to misinterpretation of statistics certain people, especially in the cities, who have not an accurate picture of the situation, have got the idea that the farmers are not too badly off after all and that their situation compares favourably with the rest of the economy. Many of these people pose as agricultural experts. I contend that they are doing the agricultural industry and farmers generally a disservice if they try to picture the industry as being prosperous or as sharing in anything like an equitable manner in the gross national product.
It was probably that sort of agriculturalist that inspired an American called Eugene Ware to say that the farmer works the soil and the agriculturist works the farmer. I should also like to point out briefly the situation as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture sees it. I shall quote a short extract from their brief entitled "Farmers meet the Cabinet". They start out by saying that generally the economy is in a healthy condition, but then they say:
On the other hand, we find that, apparently, the notable exception in this picture of record prosperity is that of the farmer and his family. We do not claim that Canadian agriculture is in a depression such as we have known in the past. We do say that the farming industry is not sharing in Canada's new high level of prosperity.
Then they go on to say this:
Farmers from coast to coast feel keenly that on the average their returns have become badly out of balance with those of other major groups in the nation. It is important to emphasize purchasing power in this connection because the farmer's difficulties are to be found as much in high prices of the things he buys as in a decline in the number of dollars he receives.
They are pointing out what I was saying just a few moments ago about the decline in the purchasing power of the dollar. That matter is extremely important. Out of the farmer's net income he must provide for his family and he must provide for a great many charges which are practically standard if he is to support on an adequate basis the community in which he lives. In that connection I should like to point out that owing to economic pressures, farm units are becoming larger. This means that in a rural community there are fewer people to carry

the load of community charges which are fixed or nearly fixed for an area. There are still churches, schools, medical assistance and many other things that must be provided for the rural area whether there are many people to pay for them or just a few.
The purchasing power of the dollar which the farmer receives is away down. City people may wonder at this statement because they have not noticed any great decline in the cost of food. As a matter of fact the cost of food to the consumer is still going up. City people generally speaking perhaps have the idea-and one should not blame them if they have-that surely the amount the farmer is receiving for what they buy is increasing also. But that is not the case, owing to the fact that the cost of distribution has risen sharply in the last few years.
For this rise in cost there are two reasons. The first is that the actual cost of distribution has gone up, and the second is the fact that consumers are demanding food in a more advanced stage of preparation as time goes by. The consumer cannot expect the farmer to be as well off when he pays for a quick-frozen T.V. meal-which one sees advertised, with a bit of chicken, some potatoes and so on, on a platter-as he would be if the same price were being paid for the ingredients of that meal. The cost of distribution and preparation is taking a larger and larger percentage of the consumer's dollar.
In that connection I note this:
Based on 15 food items, which account for about 75 per cent of consumers' expenditure on Canadian farm foods. 1955 retail prices were almost 11 per cent above 1949; for the farm equivalents of the same 15 commodities, farm prices were about 3 per cent below 1949. Marketing costs increased almost 25 per cent between these two periods while the farm share was lower by almost 9 per cent.
Farmers everywhere recognize the fact that agriculture is in an extremely trying time in its history. There have recently been great changes in production methods, and it is anticipated by many that there will be even more spectacular changes in the future in connection with methods of production and so on if agriculture is to survive. One fact, of course, is that as time goes by there are fewer and fewer farmers producing the food of the nation. This situation is brought about to a great extent by greater efficiency, larger units, mechanization and food produced in various forms from feeds that were formerly fed to horses in order to provide farm power. There are many other factors. Agriculture finds itself in an extremely difficult position.
In this economic climate there are fewer and fewer young men taking up agriculture as a career. Certainly in the agricultural

districts with which I am familiar the average age of farmers engaged in agriculture is becoming greater and greater; and as these farmers retire or die off, fewer and fewer of them are being replaced. The result is that you have large numbers of farms completely abandoned, used as pasture or cultivated to a minor extent by some farmer who lives in the vicinity. This situation puts a great load on the community because there are fewer people to support the normal community enterprises.
Of course there are some cynical people who say "So what? What difference does it make?" They say that perhaps this is a necessary thing; that it is just following the inevitable economic laws; that if that is what is happening, it is just too bad but it is an inevitable thing to which those engaged in agriculture and those who live in the country generally must face up; that they must face up to the fact that by far the greatest number of them will be exterminated in the next few years if this trend continues. I should like to warn people who have that point of view that we cannot abandon, sabotage or neglect our agricultural industry, because before too many years are past we shall need it badly and we shall need it on an efficient, high level of production. Otherwise there will be food and clothing shortages even here in North America.
The United States department of agriculture put out an extremely interesting illustrated booklet, a copy of which I have in my hand, entitled "The 5th Plate". In it they point out that, in the United States, for every four plates that were set for dinner in 1950, there will be five in 1975. Therefore there must be 25 per cent more food available for consumption in 1975 as compared with 1950. To meet this need they point out it would require all the arable land now existing in the states of Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Michigan.
They also point out that there is another way of partially meeting this need and that is to make farms, the present arable land, more productive. That can only be done, of course, if we have an economic climate in which the farmer is not forced to mine his soil to eke out a livelihood. We must have an economic climate in which he can safeguard his soil which, to the farmer, is his working capital and which is very difficult to replace.
This same booklet points out that in the United States in 1920 there were 3-62 acres of crop land for every individual in the country. By 1950 this per capita acreage had fallen to 2-25. I know these are just statistics and the city person probably does not worry too much about them because they
Supply-Agriculture
are not realities to him; they do not convey anything very real. But if you put them in terms of farming it makes the farmer realize that he has to grow food and a lot of clothing for one individual on a little over two acres of land.
That is a very difficult thing to do if you think of it in terms of sheep, cattle and horses; but when you think of it in terms of human beings it is quite a problem. We have to get away from the idea that we have an endless amount of fertile land and that there will never come a day when we cannot exploit new, fresh, virgin areas and provide an abundance of food and clothing for our inhabitants. We are getting to the point where we can no longer mine our soil in one area and then move on to fresh, fertile, virgin land when we have eroded and exploited beyond recovery the agricultural soil in a given area.
Of course, some people adopt the attitude that the answer is bigger units. That view has been put forward by at least one of our chief financial publications in this country in recent weeks. It is also the kind of thinking that induced the men in the Kremlin to set out on their program of collective farms. They took the attitude that if they had bigness, the factory type of thing, mass production, they could solve the problem. I doubt that very much. Even if it would solve the problem from a purely economic point of view, I doubt whether it is the solution we want.
I hold in my hand a full-page story that appeared in the Financial Post of April 21 this year. It contains a streamer headline which says:
Factory Farming Can Cure Our Barnyard Blues
The article reads in part:
In southwestern Saskatchewan, a dusty village squats amid rumpled hills at a point where a yellow gravel highway bumps across a single line of railroad track.
Three grain elevators-two red, one silver-tower over a rail siding. The burnt-out shell of another, never rebuilt, points blackened timbers at the sky.
A church which lost its roof to a windstorm has been abandoned. So have at least 20 houses, paint gone and yards weed-grown. Twenty years ago 306 people lived here. Now:	Only 177.
Slowly but certainly a farming community is dying.
In its own way this is a picture of agricultural progress.
This is an amazing conclusion for the writer to come to, Mr. Chairman. This is not my idea of agricultural progress.
I have another editorial which I will not bother to read, but it points out that politicians are foolish to worry about the farm bloc any more. They say that farmers are being exterminated and too much attention is

Supply-Agriculture
being given to them; that they are a dying race and that we shall soon have huge factory-like farms with only a few people operating them. They say this will be a good thing and the sooner it comes the sooner we shall have relief from this recurrent annoyance of the farm bloc demanding this or that from parliament.
I have a strong feeling that even if this is sound from the purely economic point of view, it is not sound from the sociological point of view, and that there are other things that should be taken into consideration. I ieel strongly that if our nation is to remain strong and healthy and if we are to have a large group of independent people who believe in free enterprise, and who believe in themselves, and that the world does not owe them a living but that they must earn it, we must retain the family farm.
A fine editorial on this point appeared in the Charlottetown Guardian of April 7. I do not intend to read it, but it points out, and rightly so, that this is a great problem and if our nation is to remain strong and stable the family farm must be retained, and an economic environment must be created which will permit it to remain. This is especially important in the maritimes. They also point out that in the United States something is being done about it. They say:
The same problem exists in the United States where, according to a congressional committee, more than 600,000 family farms have disappeared since 1950. There, however, steps are being taken to do something about it before it is too late. The committee which made an on the spot investigation in several farm belt states calls the family farm "the backbone of agriculture and of free enterprise in general" and warns that if it should disappear completely from the scene the strength of the nation's economy would be very seriously undermined.
I agree with that point of view most heartily. Some people take the attitude that the reason income per farm is not high is that farmers are inefficient, and they say, "You must be efficient". I point out, Mr. Chairman, there has been a great increase in the efficiency of agriculture over the years. The productiveness of the individual farmer is probably as high as that of any other member of the labouring force.
In pioneer days 90 per cent of the labour force was in agriculture. It took nine men in agriculture to provide enough to support one man in industry. At the present time the figures are reversed. Today only about one-tenth of our labour force is in agriculture, yet they still provide good food and considerable clothing for the population.
If the impression is created that agriculture is well off there is a danger that nothing will be done about it. In that connection I would
IMr. MacLean.]
like to point out that the great civilizations of the past collapsed not because of an economic collapse in the cities but because the fertility of the soil degenerated and finally disappeared. That has inevitably been the case in the past.
I think it is extremely important, Mr. Chairman, that the family farm be preserved for the reasons I have already given. In order to ensure this there are some things which I think the government should consider doing. For instance, there is the question of the customs tariff. In Canada we import a tremendous amount of fruit and vegetables from south of the border, and our balance of trade in that connection is not improving. I would like to quote briefly from a recent issue of The Grower, a trade journal, which says:
In the first nine months ol 1955 Canada imported fresh fruits and vegetables to a value of $86,973,273, a gain of $5,518,023 over the same period in 1954. In the same nine months Canada exported fresh fruits and vegetables to a value of $10,621,457, a decline of $1,739,099 over the same period in 1954. The gain in the adverse balance was therefore $7,257,122.
Further examination of the records show that imports of fresh fruits declined $740,360 whilst the imports of vegetables increased $6,258,383 for a net increase, as given, of-
That is $5 million in round figures.
There are other things, too, which I believe the government should consider doing. One is to put on the free list some additional things which are used exclusively in agriculture as recommended by the farm organizations, such as steel posts and numerous other articles which I will not detail here. In certain areas of the country encouragement should be given to the processing of food in those areas so it will be consumed there. I was shocked to read recently that of the food consumed in the four Atlantic provinces less than 30 per cent is produced there. Of course there are some exports to partly balance that, but the exports do not begin to completely balance it.
I think my time is just about up, Mr. Chairman, but I have just one more thing to say. We in the maritimes do not expect a very high rate of income, and we would go along with seeing some other sections of the country enjoying a higher income, because I think the average farmer in the maritimes realizes that farming is a way of life and is interested in preserving the family farm. If he had a choice between prairie income and scenery and maritime income and the maritime way of life he would take the latter, because he realizes that as a work of art there are few things more pleasing to the eye, or more capable of affording scope and gratification

to a taste for the beautiful, than a well-situated, well-cultivated farm.

Mr. Chairman, I was
[DOT]extremely interested in the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Queens, especially when he referred to the federation of agriculture brief in which they stated that the agricultural economy is not sharing in the high level of prosperity of the country.
Although the debate on the speech from the throne has concluded I would call to the hon. member's attention that this fact was recognized by the government when it said that some sectors of the economy have not fully participated in the country's increased wellbeing. Our government has recognized the position of agriculture, and it has done many things over the years which have been helpful to the producers. One has only to recall at the time of the foot-and-mouth disease how readily and quickly the government came to the support of the people concerned. In addition to that we have floor prices on many commodities which are produced.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Huron the other day when he asked the Minister of Labour about the possibility of getting more immigrants in this country because there is a need at this time to assist in the production on our farms.
I was rather surprised when the hon. member for Leeds got up to make his speech this afternoon and immediately started to criticize the Minister of Agriculture, indicating that he had not fully recognized the problems of agriculture in this country. He also expressed the hope that at some time they would have the opportunity of naming a minister of agriculture from eastern Ontario. May I say to him, as the Minister of Agriculture said this afternoon, we are very pleased in Ontario and throughout eastern Canada because we have the assistant to the minister who is fully conversant with all the farm problems in Ontario, in eastern Canada and in every part of Canada.
I feel a little out of character in saying what I am about to say at this time. When the Leader of the Opposition raised the point this afternoon about the Minister of Agriculture and the other ministers being absent, the Minister of Agriculture upon his return made the statement that he was out to get some facts and figures so he would be able to answer certain questions which might arise. I feel that the only reason the question of privilege was raised this afternoon was because when the Minister of Finance was replying to the amendment moved by the leader of the official opposition, and seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, at

May I ask the hon. member a question. Was he referring to the federal government's refusal to make any grants to the municipalities?
The Depuiy Chairman:	I thought I had
tried to make it clear to the committee that we are not discussing that incident or any other incident which may have taken place. We are discussing item No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

Supply-Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, speaking
more directly to the problem of agriculture I should like first to refer to an article which appeared in the Windsor Star of June 25, 1955. Speaking about the vast investment in agriculture it had this to say:
Due to the rapid industrial development of Canada there is occasional talk about the decline in importance of agriculture. This should be taken with a few grains of salt. Increases in other activities do not diminish the importance of agriculture.
It is wise to know the exact position, so there may be no misunderstanding about this. Agriculture still is far and away the principal industry in Canada. Indeed, there is more money invested in agriculture than in all manufacturing industries combined.
Most recent figures show the vast sum of $9,593,000,000 in capital investments in farm land, buildings, equipment and livestock in Canada. This compares with $8,470,000,000 in all manufacturing industries.
Even in the highly industrialized United States an authority avers there is a greater capital investment in agriculture than in all other industries combined. And it is estimated the incomes of 50 per cent of the people in the United States are derived directly or indirectly from agriculture.
These include not only farmers. Also involved are all in the canning, packing and other food processing plants. Also all in the farm implement business-manufacturing and distribution. And many in the chemical industry (suppliers of fertilizers and insecticides): in the railway and trucking industries; in the automobile and rubber factories, and in all the retail and wholesale trades handling foods.
The same would be true in Canada, possibly even more so in proportion. We produce large quantities of food for export.
It is well to put these facts in proper perspective, so that other industries-each of importance in the Canadian economy-will realize their positions.
In my opinion the problems facing agriculture in Canada are similar to the problems faced by agriculture in other countries. An article which appeared in the New York Times was headed "Has any country licked the agricultural problem?" The article goes on to deal with the $7 billion surplus which has been created by the policies followed in the United States. They mention that this was at the time the Russian agriculturists were visiting the United States-they later came to Canada-and continued:
I don't know whether the Russian agricultural experts who saw the farmers' homes had it made clear to them that some of the great farms of this country are mortgaged to the government for as high as a million dollars that the government hasn t the slightest idea of ever collecting on "loans" covered by unsalable crops. And that 43 per cent of American farmers still have net incomes of less than a thousand dollars per year-and are, in fact, paying the rich and subsidized farmers in enhanced feed prices.
It is understandable that there is a problem in the United States. An article in the Financial Times had this to say:
Moreover, under that system, the American farmer has lost all control over his major operations. Like the Russian, the American farmer is
[The Deputy Chairman.)
told exactly what, when and how much he is to grow. There is no incentive to develop new markets nor to reduce costs.
Referring to Europe the New York Times had this to say under an article headed "Farm surpluses face west Europe nations", and reading:
Efforts to get freer trade in food products within Europe have been unsuccessful.
All of us realize that the severe weather on the continent during the past winter changed that picture almost overnight and from a surplus position they soon got into a position of need. We all recall the great increase in the prices of practically every item of foodstuff which occurred. I recall the Indian delegate to the United Nations telling us last fall how they had been able to increase the production of foodstuffs in that country by the use of new cultural practices over what it had been a short time ago.
Returning to our own province, I should like to pay a compliment to the farm organizations which met in Toronto not so long ago and advocated that self-help was the best solution for any farm problem. I am proud to be associated with such people who are ready to work out a solution to a problem that may face them and try the best possible plan to bring the best possible result. They are not asking the government to pile up surpluses worth millions of dollars as has been done in the United States, to the point where they do not know how they are going to dispose of them. These surpluses have created a block to the distribution of foodstuffs in a free society such as the one in which we like to operate.
I realize that as individuals we cannot always maintain the position we would like to maintain, but our position is ever so much stronger when we act collectively. I should like to pay a compliment to the farm organizations in my own county of Kent (Ont.). We grow many specialized products in that county, and the production of many of them is organized. The production of other products is in the process of being organized. Where there is an organization you will find there is little or no problem as far as the return from that crop is concerned, but where the production is unorganized or, if you like, disorganized there is a problem because we are not always able to get the best price consistent with the cost of production.
I should like to pay a compliment to the government for the action that has been taken in connection with resolutions which have been passed from time to time by organizations in my county. These resolutions were forwarded to the ministers concerned, and while they were not always accepted, at times

the government saw fit to accept particular resolutions which had been passed. Those turned out to be favourable and to the benefit of the industry in my district or in whatever area they applied.
I would recommend to the farm organizations that they make an effort to use the established agencies for handling their products. This can be done, as has been ably demonstrated. I feel that there is a place for those people who know the selling business, because that is the important part. There is no doubt that we are able to produce to meet the needs, but we must have further organization to dispose of the products we grow.
I was very much interested this afternoon when I heard the hon. member for Queens speak about the fruits and vegetables that are imported into this country and the vegetables that we export to the United States. Certain it is that we cannot balance one type of commodity with a similar type of commodity, but if we did we would be denying the Canadian people the right to make the choice they would like to make as far as fruits and vegetables are concerned. But we do attempt as best we can to meet the problems that face us.
I should like now to offer a suggestion to the government that I feel will be helpful to an industry in my district. I refer to the corn industry. In looking over the figures I note that at one time the production of corn in this country was very minor in extent. I have figures only for the province of Ontario, but I believe the greater proportion of the corn grown in Canada for commercial purposes is grown within this province.
In 1940 we had a production of nearly 7 million bushels of shelled corn. In 1955 that production had increased to the point where we were growing nearly 32 million bushels.
I take a great deal of satisfaction in knowing that the county from which I come and which I have the honour to represent has extended its production from 2 million bushels in 1940 to nearly 11 million bushels in 1955. We have increased our average yield on a provincial basis from 37-4 to 62-6 bushels per acre. That is an increase of 70 per cent for the province. The figures for the county of Kent (Ont.) show an increase in the same period of over 80 per cent.
I heard the hon. member for Queens read an article stating the concern of some people about the arable land being used up, and expressing some concern as to whether we shall be able to meet the needs of our people in the foreseeable future. I for one do not believe that situation will ever occur, because at this moment our provincial average production of corn is 62-6 bushels per acre.
Supply-Agriculture
During 1955 a 4-H club member produced 304-38 bushels per acre. I feel that in the future we shall continue to improve as we have done in the past.
One of the ways in which I think we might be able to help this industry in my district is this. Corn coming in from the United States bears an 8 cents tariff. If we were to ship com into the United States it would have a tariff of 25 cents a bushel. The tariff was established at a time when we were not selfsufficient in the production of corn. Today Canadians produce the amount of corn needed by our people, and we are exporting some corn as well. Some time ago I made representations, along with the hybrid seed corn producers of our district. On that occasion, on a presidential prerogative, the tariff against seed corn going into the United States was reduced by one-half, and there are further representations being made that the executive exercise its right of reducing it at the rate of 5 per cent for three consecutive years if it so chooses. That would be helpful.
I should like to recite a specific case. At a given point in my district, 76 miles from London, where the great Kellogg plant is located, corn going over the railroad bears a tariff of 25J cents. But corn can come from Chicago, a distance of 376 miles, and cost only 5 cents more to haul, and it is being hauled under arrangements that were made quite some years ago. I would suggest to the minister, and also to the Minister of Transport that they give consideration to looking into the rates that apply on this commodity. We have the Crowsnest pass and the maritime rates and we have the bridge over northern Ontario. If our railroads are to be used in the national interest, I suggest that it would be in the national interest if something were done for this industry, which plays a very important part in the Canadian economy.
There is another item to which I should like to refer, and that is the item of soybeans. We are not self-sufficient in that commodity. We started to grow them only in 1942. In my own county we produced 308,000 bushels in 1942, and in 1955 we produced 2,034,300 bushels. Our total production in Canada for 1955 was 5-65 million bushels. Along with that, Canada has the highest yield of any country. The average United States yield is 20-2 bushels per acre. In Ontario it is 26 bushels per acre, and the county I have the privilege of representing has an average of 29-7 bushels per acre.
Soybeans come into this country free, but if we want to export them to the United States they cost $1.20 a bushel. When that tariff was established that was perfectly all right, because we needed the soybeans from

Supply-Agriculture
the United States if our crushing plants in this country were to be established. Today we have them established and, though we are net yet self-sufficient, I am sure the time is rapidly approaching when we can produce all that is necessary. Again we have the rail problem, and it is almost identical with that connected with corn except that it has one more feature. It has a different classification. It is classified under oil seeds and bears a higher freight tariff than corn. So, in addition to possibly reclassification which is necessary, this product should be put on a basis that would enable us to meet the competition from abroad.
The reason I bring up the question of rail rates is this. In Toledo, which is just across the lake from our crushing plants, the soybeans can be loaded into lake boats or barges and taken across the lake. They go across at a rate of 6 to 7 cents a bushel. In our case, to ship soybeans from Chatham, from where I come, costs 25 cents a bushel. Therefore our people are at a disadvantage of 18 to 19 cents a bushel. If we can overcome this disadvantage we will be in a very favourable position to increase our production and meet our competitors, the producers in the United States. For that reason I trust that the government will pay some attention to this aspect of the problem.
There is one other matter, and this one really brings tears to my eyes because I wish to speak about onions. Last year we had an exceptionally good crop of onions in my district but the farmers of New York state lost their onions because of severe floods. The growers of my district generously offered eight carloads of onions to the producers in New York state. The only requirement was that they would sell the onions and distribute the funds among the people of New York state. However, the government of the United States would not waive the regulations that applied, and consequently the gift could not be accepted. I hope that in the representations made to Washington from time to time these problems will be taken care of so that we can meet any competition there may be.
There is another problem with regard to onions. There is a duty of 37J cents on onions coming into Canada from the United States, and during certain periods of the year they come in free. On Canadian onions going into the United States the duty is 75 cents. Our people feel they can produce equally as well as any other country, and all they are asking is that the United States put their tariff in line with our tariff and allow us an equal opportunity to compete wherever the market may be. Our people will be satisfied if that is done. I think that is a compliment

to the ability of our people to produce, and that is what they would like to see the government do.
I should like to refer to an article that appeared in the London Free Press reporting an address by Frank E. Wolff, chairman of the agriculture committee of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in the course of which he said that food was the greatest weapon. I agree that is the case. I should like to pay a particular compliment to our plant breeders and cerealists who over the years have introduced types of plants and grains that have increased production and have given people in many parts of the world the opportunity to eat better than they ever did before. I would say that our plant breeders, cerealists, agronomists and others connected with such work have rendered a greater service to mankind than the physicists and other scientists.
We all know what happens when an atom or hydrogen bomb is exploded over an atoll. A chain reaction starts in Moscow. They say they have a bigger and better bomb, and that they exploded it first. I should like to tell you what has been done in my district by our plant breeders and cerealists. They have produced a hybrid seed corn which has increased production from the figure of around 40 bushels an acre that I mentioned a while ago to a maximum of 304 bushels an acre. When the Russian delegation were here they purchased hybrid seed corn from my district. It is going to their country and possibly it will have an effect so far as the Russian people are concerned. There is one thing of which I am sure. I am confident that a Canadian kernel is much better than a Russian kernel.
