speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on this occasion to support a resolution passed unanimously at the twelfth annual convention of the Ontario canning crop growers at Hamilton, Ontario, on December 1, 1955. The purpose of the resolution was to recommend to the government that a pilot processing plant be established at the Smithfield horticultural substation. As Smithfield is in the riding of Northumberland which I have the pleasure to represent I think I can point' out many reasons why Smithfield is the logical place for the establishment of such a pilot processing plant. The association represents some 10,000 growers of vegetable canning crops in the province of Ontario. The resolution is worded as follows:
Be it resolved that this convention request the Canada Department of Agriculture to establish a pilot processing plant at the Smithfield horticultural

substation of the Canada Department of Agriculture for the purpose of further studying the relationship of raw product grades to those in the finished product grades of processing crops and that sufficient commercial acreage be grown at the above station to supply the pilot plant with the raw product of the crops being studied.
The resolution was supported by a brief which was presented to the deputy minister of agriculture on February 15 of this year. I should like to express the appreciation of all members of this organization for the courtesy of the deputy minister of agriculture and the sympathetic hearing he gave to the delegation. In supporting the brief I feel I can do no better than to quote very briefly from the brief itself in order to demonstrate the requirement for and purpose and need of such a pilot processing plant. The brief as presented to the deputy minister reads in part as follows under the heading "The Need":
By reason of its location, weather conditions at the central experimental farm at Ottawa are not ideal for the growing of many of the major canning crops. In recognition of this fact, the Canada Department of Agriculture some years ago established a horticultural substation at Smith-field, Ontario, to permit the study of problems encountered by growers of fruits and vegetables under actual conditions existing in one of Canada's important areas of production of these crops, particularly for the food processing industry. . . .
To be of practical value to agriculture and the food processing industry, fruit and vegetable varieties must possess qualities that enable both producers and processors to market food products that meet with consumer acceptance. The grower has to produce a crop of high quality and yield which he can produce and market at a reasonable profit. The objective of the food processor in respect to the finished product is identical. At the same time, consumers demand, in this era of keen competition both in price and variety of food products, processed food products of good flavour, colour, texture, odour and generally attractive appearance.
I go on further in the brief, and under the heading, "The Purpose" there is the following:
A food products laboratory should be established at Smithfield, Ontario, in order to help the plant breeder, the grower, the processor and the consumer. . . . Such a laboratory would provide the facilities for objective testing and evaluation of various varieties of fruits and vegetables produced on the substation acreage.
Later, results could be discussed with plant breeders and ultimately, when a variety is considered ready for commercial introduction, results and performance could be discussed with producers and processors in order to assure industry acceptance of the results of research in a minimum of time.
. . . For optimum quality of the finished product, a promising variety must be harvested at a definite maturity and processed by a definite procedure that can be carefully controlled. A food processing laboratory at Smithfield would provide the means of determining the desirable maturity and establishing a definite processing procedure for a given variety.
Supply-Agriculture
In addition, the laboratory could conduct research to determine the reasons for: flavour loss in processing, loss of colour intensity, undesirable odour development and texture characteristics of processed food products. As a further practical contribution to the industry and the economy,, such a laboratory would enable research authorities to develop new types of processed foods that would channel commodities which might at any time in the future be in surplus supply into the consumer market.
Finally, under the heading of "Requirements" of such a plan the following has been suggested:
In order to provide the facilities for such research, it is respectfully suggested that the-laboratory at Smithfield consist of:
(1)	a pilot plant.
(2)	a laboratory for evaluation.
(3)	cold storage and freezer facilities.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to support this brief wholeheartedly because I am sure that in Smithfield we have all the requirements for the establishment of a successful pilot processing plant. I also know that the Ontario food processors' association feel the need for such a pilot plant so they may carry on extensive research on food products in this industry. They also feel that Smithfield is an ideal location for such a plant because technical personnel from Ottawa could avail themselves of the opportunity of conducting on the spot research in a major canning area in Canada, thus eliminating the necessity for recruiting additional technical staff which would be necessary if such a pilot processing plant were established in another area in Canada.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, among both growers and processors there is a feeling that since Ontario is the major centre of canning crop production, the province of Ontario is the logical place for the establishment of such a pilot processing plant. If the Department of Agriculture can give sympathetic consideration to this suggestion I am sure we shall be providing an extremely valuable service which will be of benefit not only to the growers of fruits and vegetables in Canada but also to the processing industry and ultimately to the consuming public itself.

Mr. Chairman, I believe this is something of a notable day in the House of Commons, in that members of all political parties have risen in their places and said to the government that all was not well with the agricultural industry. I am most happy to see members on the government side of the house-Liberal members, in this case Liberal members from Ontario-rising and pointing out to the government that substantial improvements are necessary in its agricultural policy.
As everyone knows, in this nation today we are witnessing an increase in our wealth

Supply-Agriculture
production. In recent years we have had an almost uninterrupted increase in the general production of this country. But anyone viewing the important segment of the Canadian economy cannot help but come to the conclusion that agriculture is the one important segment that is not sharing in any way in this general rise in prosperity. As a matter of fact instead of improving its position agriculture is going down, and it has been going down for some years. Moreover, the position of agriculture is not falling at a small, imperceptible rate; it is falling at a most alarming rate.
I have here figures obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics. They show that the gross cash income for agriculture was $2,811 million in 1951 and that it has been falling steadily until in 1955 it is estimated that gross cash incomes for agriculture will be some $2,323 million. The net income position is much worse. There is a drop from $2,150 million in 1951 to $1,125 million in 1954. That is a drop of some 48 per cent within that three-year period.
I do not believe our so-called prosperous economy can be secure as long as we have this important segment with inadequate purchasing power and with falling standards of living. During this period to which I have referred the gross national product has increased from $21-4 billion in 1951 to $26-4 billion in 1955. Some may think that, as consumers, they stand to gain if prices of food products fall. In its brief to the Gordon commission the Canadian Federation of Agriculture points out that in many years when agricultural prices are falling the cost of food products to the consumer is increasing. It does not follow at all that because farm prices are falling to the producer, the consumer is gaining in any way. I am afraid the consumer will stand to lose by any further deterioration in the position of agriculture.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was pointing out that while most sections of our economy were relatively prosperous, agriculture was in no way sharing in that prosperity. Not only have farm cash income and farm net income been going down, but probably of greater significance is the fact that the prices of agricultural products in relation to the farmer's costs of production have been continually getting worse.

Shortly after the Minister of Agriculture took office back in 1935 there was established an index for the farm costs of production and for farm prices. The base of that index was taken as 1935-39. That period was taken as 100 for the farmer's cost of production and for the prices of agricultural products. The latest index based on that period as set out in the Economic Annalist for April, 1956, shows that the prices of farm products have increased to 218. But the cost of production index has gone up until it has not only reached 218 but has gone even higher until it stands at 235. According to the Economic Annalist, the prices of agricultural products today in relation to the farmer's cost of production are even lower than they were in the depressed years from 1935 to 1939. That is why we in this group say it is time the government adopted a price support policy based on parity, that is prices for agricultural products that bear a fair relationship to the farmer's cost of production.
An important announcement was made today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that will affect agriculture on the prairies and indirectly all parts of Canada. We welcome that part of the announcement concerning the 1956-57 initial prices for grain. We also welcome the statement that within about two weeks' time an announcement will be made as to the final payment on the 1954 wheat crop. But there was a third announcement that was highly disturbing to me, namely the announcement that at the end of the current crop year delivery quotas for grain to various points would not be equalized, that no steps would be taken by the Canadian wheat board or by the government to bring about an equalization of quotas.
That statement will not sit very well on the western prairies. I am afraid there will be a tremendous amount of criticism. I am afraid that in the natural course of events people who support the Winnipeg grain exchange will use this new policy as a weapon against the Canadian wheat board. I express the hope that between now and the end of the crop year the government will give serious reconsideration to the statement that was made this afternoon and change it so that quotas are equalized among producers at various marketing points. If it is impossible to equalize them on July 31, whatever quotas some farmers may be short of at that time should be extended into the new crop year.
I am for parity prices; I am for a price level that would give agriculture a fair share of the national income. But within a system of parity prices for agricultural prices I also

believe that steps should be taken to bring about the greatest practicable equalization of income amongst the farmers themselves. That is why I am so disturbed over the announcement this afternoon that even on an acreage basis there will be unequal quotas during the crop year and nothing will be done at the snd of the crop year to see that those quotas are equalized. I repeat, I hope the government will reconsider its policy and will bring about an equalization of grain delivery quotas.
A few years ago when one stood up in the house and advocated a system of parity prices one perhaps did not get too much vocal support from farm organizations; but every single farm organization of any importance, and every farm organization in Canada with which I am acquainted, is advocating some system of guaranteed support prices or some system of parity prices. The great Canadian Federation of Agriculture has brought before the government a policy advocating fair relationship prices, advocating that the government implement a system of support prices that will guarantee to the farmer not less than from 65 per cent to 85 per cent of a parity price. The interprovincial farm union council, in making their submission to the government every year and in making their submission to the agriculture committee of the house, has emphasized its position that the farmers should have parity prices. The government has done very little or nothing about those submissions.
We have a reasonably good support price for butter, but after you have said that there is little more to say. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is highly respected in this nation. Hope was discussing agricultural policies generally and what his organization wished the government to do, I asked him this question, as recorded at page 114 of the proceedings of the committee:

bother about agriculture at all? After all, it is an industry of dwindling importance; after all, it is losing its political power and effect in the nation. Be it further resolved that our new congress strives, through the recently-created Canadian farm-labour economic council, to unite the forces of farmers and labour in Canada, for the welfare of both sections of the population and the country as a whole.

Whereas this convention views with alarm the ruinous drop in agricultural income . . . and

Whereas we join with organized farmers in their farm unions, co-operatives, and with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in their fight to obtain parity for the agricultural producer:

Be it resolved that, to this end, efforts be made to regain the overseas markets that have been lost to Canadian farmers since the end of world war II; an immediate campaign to eliminate malnutrition in Canada be launched; a generous program of economic assistance be undertaken to help fight world poverty and hunger, and a generous program of support prices be established, so that both producers and consumers will be protected from violent fluctuations in price and supply.

Sixth, support for an international food pool to dispose of surplus agricultural products. Seventh, double the payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and extend the act to provide income protection in time of crop failure for farmers in all parts of Canada. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act was first brought into existence in 1939 and provided a maximum of $2.50 per acre on half the cultivated acreage. That payment has not been increased, even though the cost of production has more than doubled since that time. I suggest that the payment should be doubled and the provisions of the act should be extended to agricultural producers in all parts of Canada in the case of crop failure.
Eighth, extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all parts of Canada, making it into a comprehensive program of soil and water conservation. Ninth, immediate construction of the South Saskatchewan dam. It used to be that the Prime Minister would discuss in this house the benefits or otherwise, depending upon his point of view, which would flow from the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam, but now when he is asked a question he just says no. There is no argument, there is no consideration; the government says no. It might cost a little over $60 million from the federal treasury to build this dam, but apparently there is no hesitation in providing $80 million to pull a pipe-line company out of a very bad situation into which it is getting and in which it apparently wants to involve the country as well. And I added:

the provincial government have been one-third respectively, with the other third being paid by the farmers. There are 13,382 maple sugar producers who have taken advantage of that opportunity to change their pails, out of a possible total of 21,700, always according to the 1951 census.

Canadian poultry producers would be buying more grain to feed their poultry if it were not for those importations, and it would help to reduce the

surplus of grain in the western provinces. This is a product that Canadians can produce.
What about the duty? The poultry people asked for a duty of 12J per cent, as now, but with a minimum of 5 cents a pound. This is identical with the United States tariff on eviscerated turkeys. However, on dressed turkeys the United States rate is 10 cents a pound; hence the Canadian proposal is a moderate one. I suggest that the government give further consideration to the problem.
I hold in my hand an editorial from the Montreal Gazette of today. The editorial is based on a pamphlet issued by the Canadian institute of international affairs. It is entitled, "What is Happening to Wheat?" I have been critical at times of the length of time and the number of speeches that have been devoted to wheat in this house, but the western economy and in fact the Canadian economy are tied up with it. This is one of the things the Canadian institute of international affairs had to say:
But the conclusion remains inconclusive. "Looking into the tunnel of the future of wheat sales," the writers admit, "it must be conceded that no light is visible".
In other words, there does not seem to be any answer to this problem of recurring wheat surpluses. For some time we have been a wheat exporting country, but many of the countries to whom we exported wheat are now exporters themselves. Instead of being importers they are now exporters and that aggravates the situation. Agriculture in Canada needs more to be diversified than at any time in its history. Some guidance and some assurances are required from the government before the farmers in large numbers are going to switch from one type of agriculture to another. There must be some guidance, some continuity of markets before they make the switch.
I also hold in my hand an editorial from the Sarnia Observer which is entitled, "The Sad Sugar Beet Story". There are many acres in Manitoba and Alberta that are suitable for the production of sugar beets. In southwestern Ontario we have been growing sugar beets for many years. There are two sugar beet factories in southwestern Ontario, one at Chatham and the other at Wallaceburg. I understand that one of these plants will not operate this year. Yet we have acres of land that could be devoted to the production of sugar, an article we import. The use of those acres for this purpose would take wheat off the market and put sugar on the market. The farmers who have been engaged in sugar beet growing in the past have done fairly well. Yet we drift and lose the sugar beet industry that we have built up. The sugar beet plants in southwestern Ontario

require at least 30,000 or 40,000 acres of sugar beets to operate economically and well. So far this year only 19,000 acres of sugar beets are contracted for in southwestern Ontario.
We as a people are prepared to delegate authority to groups without giving the matter sufficient consideration. If there is one agricultural product produced in this country that I know anything about it is honey. It has had its ups and downs so far as production and prices are concerned during the last few years. For many years Canada has been an exporting nation, but now she has drifted into the column of the importing nations so far as honey is concerned. Our importations are now running around 5 million pounds a year, but we used to export a great deal more than that each year.
In many of the provinces co-operative companies are set up by the honey producers to process and market the honey of their producer members. One of the astounding things to me is this. The Canadian beekeepers' council, in co-operation with the managers of those co-operatives, has brought enough pressure to bear on the dominion Department of Agriculture to have the words that designate the country of origin of the honey removed from the containers. It is no longer necessary for a Canadian packer of honey to put on the container how much, if any, foreign honey is in the container. That is working against the Canadian producers of honey. Those very co-operatives that were supposed to serve the interests of the producer are among the importers of this foreign honey.
As I say, they have brought pressure to bear on the dominion department to have that grading and marketing regulation changed. I hold in my hand copies of the letters that have to do with it. I notice that the province of Quebec particularly protested very strongly against changing the regulations. According to the regulations as they now exist all that has to be put on a carton of honey that holds 12 or 24 pails is the country of origin; but when it reaches the grocer's shelves it is marked as Canadian honey, and even the word "Canadian" can be removed. As I say, we delegate too much authority to certain people and do not follow it up to see what they are doing.
There is another thing the Department of Agriculture should look into. Some time ago I asked that the tenders for milk for the veterans' hospital at London, Ontario, be tabled. One of the dairies tendered a rather low price. That is all right, but this is what happened. Immediately the district purchasing agent at Kingston had this to say, and I quote from a letter from the Department of 67509-226
Supply-Agriculture
Defence Production signed by Frank Power, district purchasing agent, 953 Somerset street west, Ottawa. He wrote to Mr. Fred Burnette, secretary of the milk distributors at Kingston, Ontario.
Our headquarters have been checking the milk prices paid in this area and in view of the fact that the dairies in Ottawa and Picton are supplying the army with fresh milk at $0.57 per gallon, they have instructed us to write you and request that you give serious and immediate consideration to the high price you are charging for fresh milk in Kingston.
As soon as this one dairy tendered at a low price to get into the market in London, Ontario, the effect was going to be siphoned back to the suppliers of fresh milk in every area in the country, apparently, because this took place very shortly after the tender was received in London.

of me one portion of the minister's speech reported at page 1061 of Hansard, which reads as follows:
Good farmers in Saskatchewan, since we have had income taxes to pay, carry their wheat along knowing that they can average their income over the years-
-and so on. Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to take up the time of the house by quoting a lot of statistics that have already been quoted. I believe my colleague the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose and many other hon. members have given statistics that prove conclusively that the plight of agriculture is not a happy one.
Statistics are always extremely interesting, particularly when they relate to the part of agriculture that is closest to one's heart. Being associated with the livestock industry for a number of years it is always interesting for me to find out what is going on. Generally speaking the statistics to which I refer relate to the number of livestock produced and their gross sales value, broken down as to various types and grades and of course the unit prices that relate thereto.
Generally speaking, many of the people who are engaged in the livestock industry seem to accept these statistics as inevitable. They appear to take it for granted that it is an act of fate that we have substandard grades. I believe this is partly due to the unrealistic thinking of some of those engaged in the agricultural business. I cannot bring my reasoning to coincide with those who feel that they can forever produce substandard foundation stock and expect' to get top grades. I think that is one of the common faults of many livestock producers today. In that respect I believe we contribute considerably to our own plight, and if that is so I think another thing must be taken into consideration.
Many people today, particularly those who are not established in agriculture or livestock producing, feel that it is beyond the financial ability of the livestock producers to go out and buy No. 1 breeding stock. This is reflected in many ways. First of all it is reflected in the grade the producer receives, and it is also reflected in the over-all standard of the dominion as a whole.
I believe it would be worth while for the government to make available to those in
[The Chairman.]
that position certain sums of money in order that they may provide a proper foundation stock. It may be argued, of course, that such money is already available through farm loans. I do not know how it applies, but my experience with farm loans is that by the time they take care of the other apparently more urgent needs there is nothing left to apply to proper foundation stock. I do not know exactly what attitude the government would take, but I believe that charity begins at home, and I think that would be one way whereby the government could greatly assist with a minimum of expense.
There are other things which contribute to the plight of the livestock grower. When he takes his stock to market he receives top grades in some cases but in many cases he receives substandard grade. Another matter which is worthy of consideration is the ill-advised practice followed by those charged with processing, particularly pork. It is a well known fact that after these products are processed and marketed many inferior grades masquerade under a first-grade banner or brand. I think I can say with safety that you can go into nine out of ten meat stores in this city and discover that this is the case. If the government would be a little more careful in its inspections it would be of benefit to the over-all economy of the country.
I think we took a step in the right direction last session when we ruled out of the picture striped wrapping for bacon. That was something which was very necessary at that time, but I think we left as a substitute for it something which is perhaps even more vicious. It has been my experience since coming here this session to find, masquerading as No. 1 back bacon, meat which is nothing but No. 4 sow back bacon. True, it had the fat trimmed off and looked rather good to the unsuspecting public, but in reality it was still sow bacon. I have bought bacon myself wrapped as No. 1 which proved to be at least No. 2. Then you will find hams which by no stretch of the imagination could be qualified as No. 1. They may be split into perhaps three pieces, but are wrapped in attractive packages and sold at No. 1 prices.
These are some of the things that could be done to help the consuming public and at the same time allow the farmer, the ultimate consumer, to buy back his own products at a fair price. These things may not appear to be important, but I think they are. It is the easy things of this kind that we can do in order to get back to a more realistic sense of duty and responsibility. So long as we permit these unfair business tactics to prevail we will be falling short of our responsibility as members of parliament.

Then so far as the beef industry is concerned there are many merchants-this is more characteristic of the big merchants- who are ready to charge a price without having any sense of the true value. It may be that I am more critical than some, but I always try to keep my eyes open to see what the other fellow is doing in my own business. I have found many cases where the true grade is not represented. The article is put into an attractive package and a price charged which is far beyond the true value. To me that is nothing less than racketeering, and I think it is high time we did something about it.
There are many who feel that the government must take full responsibility for everything in connection with agriculture, but I think we should be realistic enough to know that there are contributing factors. The price of meat is regulated by many factors, the weather being one. If the roads are bad and the supply is short inevitably the price goes up, or the reverse can happen. I believe that if we would try to deal with these simple things which are within the realm of possibility we would do a lot. It is simply a matter of carrying out regulations which exist already. There is a body of inspectors who are supposed to check these things. Someone must be falling down on the job, because it is quite obvious what is happening. You do not have to go very far before you find these things which are anything but right and fair.
So far as assistance in the purchasing of proper foundation stock is concerned, that to me would seem to be one of the easiest things to do. As far as the actual dollars and cents are concerned, it would cost the government next to nothing and I am sure it would pay huge dividends.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a few minutes to express some of my thoughts on agriculture and to do something which I have not done since about 1950 or 1951; that is, to express the pride which I have in agriculture as it is practised in Durham county, from which I come. I have been most interested in listening this afternoon and this evening, as well as the other times we have been dealing with these estimate':, to the extremely well-prepared and well-presented addresses dealing with agricultural problems as well as the many suggestions that have been made.
I should like to pay a real and sincere tribute to my good friend and colleague the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture, who has been handling the estimates for part of this afternoon and this 67509-2264
Supply

Agriculture
evening. In my opinion he is as well qualified to deal with these matters as any hon. member on the opposition side, if not better. Over the years he has done a terrific job for agriculture in Ontario and throughout Canada, as has his minister. We are proud of him and we congratulate him.
I want to congratulate the Department of Agriculture and the government upon their agricultural policies over the years. I have no apologies to make, either to my own people back home or to anyone in Canada, for the agricultural policies which have been pursued by this government for a period of some 20 years. A tremendous job has been done for agriculture.
Undoubtedly everyone, and this would include the Minister of Agriculture and his cabinet colleagues, will admit that at the present time there are soft spots in agriculture. I would be the first to admit that. I have a letter which I received today from a good friend in Durham county who is engaged in agriculture. The main point he brings up is that hon. members of this house, and especially the member for Durham, should continue to put forward the agricultural position so the urban people may understand the difficulties which agriculture must face. I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Assiniboia suggest that the neswpapers across Canada do not present a fair picture of agriculture and its problems to their readers. I wish he had qualified that statement by referring only to urban newspapers.
I said most of the big city dailies.

It so happens that I have some connection with a weekly newspaper, of which there are some 900 in Canada. I can assure the hon. members of this house that the weekly newspapers are most conscious of the problems facing the agricultural people of this country. Over the years they have done a great deal to support them in their activities. I repeat that I wish the hon. member had qualified his statement. I do not want to condemn all daily newspapers, as I know there are some which appreciate and understand the problems of agriculture, but others seem more inclined to think of the high prices the city people might have to pay if agriculture received the prices it is entitled to receive.
To deal just for a moment with agriculture in Durham county, we are very proud of our agriculturists, as I have said. There may be objection to this from some quarters, but we feel that without any doubt we have the finest apples there are in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Pardon?

Supply-Agriculture

I am glad to see that the hon. member for Grey North is taking exception to that, because he made some disparaging remarks when talking about his own county's apples some time ago, and I am just handing it back to him.
What about some samples?

You had samples a few years ago, and I know everyone enjoyed them to the full. One of the finest proofs, if you like, that the apples we have in Durham county are of a superlative type was given at the last Royal Winter Fair, when an excellent farmer and apple grower, Wilfred Carruthers, and his son, from Bowmanville, practically swept all the top prizes at that fair in apple growing.
Conservatives.

I hesitate to say anything in response to someone who is injecting "Conservatives", because I am quite well aware that, in this case especially, there are good Conservative apple growers in Durham county as well.
The socialist apple would have a worm in it.
But the prize ones happen to have been grown this year by a family of good Liberals.
You mean there are good ones?

I wish to pay tribute to Mr. Carruthers, and his wife and son for the excellent job they did. There is another field in which Durham county has excelled for many years. It comes under the heading of the agricultural representative. Our agricultural representative is a man by the name of Ed Summers, who has been there for some 26 years now. He has done one of the most remarkable jobs I have seen or anybody else has seen. His judging teams of young farmers have swept practically all the prizes throughout Ontario and, indeed, he and his teams, especially his seed grain judging team, established a record of 26 consecutive victories in the district competition, which I believe has never been equalled, nor will it be equalled in your lifetime or mine.
I also wish to pay tribute to the many other fine farmers we have in Durham county. Some of them are doing remarkably well. Some of them are following the trend that is outlined in the Financial Post, of gradually obtaining more and more land and, in this industrialization of farming, converting their

small acreage into large operations. I believe those people are doing remarkably well and will continue to do so.
Some of the small farmers are not doing as well as one would like them to be doing. Undoubtedly there are many marginal farmers who are working hard but not getting the results from their efforts that they should. We are in a rather unique part of Canada in that we have an excellent farming community and right alongside we have the great plants of General Motors, Goodyear and so on, down through to Port Hope, where we have the Mathews Conveyer Company Limited, Nicholson File Company, Port Hope Sanitary Manufacturing Company Limited, and many other plants. Those plants have employees who are receiving excellent wages, almost top wages within Canada. It is very difficult for the farmers of my area to resist the temptation to leave their farms, being lured to the towns where those industries are paying, as I have said, top wages throughout Canada. But many of them are staying on the farms and continuing the lives their fathers and grandfathers led before them, in the hope that farming will continue to provide their livelihood for the remainder of their lives. I have one friend who went through college, came to work in Ottawa for a while in one of the departments, then returned to his father's farm and took it over. He appears to be sincerely enjoying that type of life. It is a type of living that one cannot get from the factories or in the urban communities.
As I have said, I have no apologies to make for this government's farm policy. I have seen it progress throughout the years. I have seen the great demands-what I would almost call the irresponsible demands-from the opposition benches. According to their words, those members would quite willingly give pie in the sky to everyone in Canada. They have no responsibility for carrying it out. I dare say if they were on the government benches they would not carry out one-eighth of what they have said in this house.
Fortunately in this country we have a government which is most interested in agriculture and in every other part of the economy. We have a responsible government, a government which is responsible not only to the city-dwelling taxpayers but also to the rural taxpayers, a government which is carrying out that responsibility to the best of its ability and upon the advice of the many farm organizations across Canada. We have seen from the many briefs we have received that in the main the agricultural organizations back this government's policy to the full. Certainly they want more than this government is able to do at the present time or feels it should do at the present time.

I believe that holds true for practically every member who has rural constituents and who is interested in farm policies. We too are constantly urging the government to do more, and we have the same sense of responsibility some of the opposition speakers seem to have. We would probably be on our feet screaming our heads off about how dreadful conditions are on our farms and how poor those farmers are, and screaming to high heaven for parity prices-120 per cent parity prices, if you like-
That would not be parity.

You would not take 120? I am glad to hear that. They have had 90 and 75, and it is very difficult to know just where they end. However, as I have said, we Liberals too are most interested in the farm policies of Canada. We are most interested in farmers and in their welfare-
And their votes.

-and we are constantly urging the government to take further steps along these lines. We have seen at least two improvements this session, with the extension of the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the extension in the general farm loan legislation. I feel quite certain that this improvement is going to continue until we have agriculture at the level where the government thinks it should be and the farmers throughout this country feel it should be.
I was most interested again in the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia, who has a very peculiar concept of what should be done in Canada. He seems to feel, as indeed some farm organizations and some farmers throughout Canada seem to feel, that there is only one way to lick the problem of farm surpluses and other problems of the farm economy, and that is for farmers throughout Canada to join with labour and form a great pressure group which could automatically elect a complete government of labour and farm people which would automatically do everything for labour and the farmers. If you follow his thinking far enough, it would do nothing for anybody else.
I cannot quite see the day coming when that kind of pressure politics would be accepted as a normal thing in our Canadian political system, and I hope it never happens. We represent the people of our areas here as best we know how and we shall continue to do so. I am quite confident that the government will remain in office on the strength of the votes of farmers who will support the policies that have been enacted over the years and that will be enacted for their benefit on a responsible basis in future years.
Supply-Agriculture
I was most interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia when he quoted Dr. Hope, the economist of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, as saying that this government was doing less than any other government in the world for its farmers. Peculiarly enough I had read an article by Dr. Hope some time earlier, at one of the federation of agriculture meetings I have attended over the years. The article is to be found in the January issue of The Country Guide. This well known economist made a very good survey of the problem of the squeeze on farmers. I should like to read a part of what he said, which shows quite definitely that Dr. Hope, as an economist with considerable knowledge of this problem and with no political bias, shall we say, did not blame the situation of the farmers on the federal government of Canada as so many speakers have done tonight. Dr. Hope, who should and I believe does know his subject, and who is also more interested in the farmers than possibly most people here, had this to say:
International trade in farm products, which rose steadily from 1946 to 1951, has now levelled off and is not increasing. Countries which, a few years ago, needed to import large quantities of food products, are now requiring less or, in some cases, have even become large exporters of some products. Examples of the latter are France and Turkey, which are now net exporters of wheat. This drying up of export demand from countries outside of North America has seriously affected the export trade in farm products for Canada and the United States . . .
In this article, Dr. Hope goes on to say that one of the main reasons for the decline in farm income from 1951 onward is the very point made in the quotation I have read, the surplus of agricultural products throughout the world, including Canada and the United States. If you accept Dr. Hope's opinion on the one score, surely you will be willing to accept his opinion on the other.
May I say again to hon. members and to my constituents back home that I shall continue my efforts while in the house to have done for the farm economy of Canada everything I feel can responsibly be done. I will also bring every effort to bear on the cabinet if I feel they are not doing enough, and will bring that same effort to bear in encouraging them to continue the policies-
Which policy?
-they have followed for many years and to improve-
Which policy?

-as we go on the policies of this government and the Liberal party throughout Canada. I am sure that in the end the farmers will fare far better than

Supply-Agriculture
they would if they entrusted their luck to the peculiar sense of responsibility evidenced by the Conservative, C.C.F., or Social Credit parties in this house.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Durham. He spoke of the great apple growing industry in his constituency and I am sure it is every bit as good as he says it is. I do not know whether he is an apple grower himself, but he surely qualifies as an apple polisher. He did a splendid job tonight.
I was rather intrigued with his argument that agriculture is well off under present Liberal policy, but I think a cold, unemotional look at the statistics is perhaps more indicative than the kind of speech we have just heard. When we look at the statistics and find that the almost 20 per cent of the Canadian population engaged in agriculture last year received less than 7 per cent of the national income, then I am afraid my hon. friend will have to revise some of his opinions with regard to the prosperity of agriculture generally.
However, it is not my intention to follow the line he has taken. I want to refer this evening to a few matters that come under the administration of the Department of Agriculture and try to get answers to some of the questions we have been asking for a number of sessions. I wish to begin with one of the acts administered by the department, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. My colleague the hon. member for Selkirk has on many occasions brought up in the house the problem of the application of that act as it affects his constituency, and there are many other areas in the province of Manitoba which are similarly affected.
At this time I should like to make a plea to the parliamentary assistant, who is piloting these estimates through, and to the government generally to have a second look at the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. In the speech from the throne at the beginning of the session we were advised that amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act would be coming forward this session. Later in the session, in reply to a question from this side of the house, the Minister of Agriculture stated that the government had changed their minds and that there would be no amendments to the act during this session. I am hoping they will change their minds again, because if we have crop losses in the prairie provinces on the same scale or anything approaching the scale of 1955 we are going to find that the act will

again be a most inadequate instrument to compensate the farmers for the losses they will suffer.
There are a number of things wrong with the act, and I should like to point out three of them. First of all there is the question of picking out eligible blocks. We know it has been difficult enough to qualify under the act at any time. A few years ago an amendment was passed by parliament making an eligible block an irregular block, that is making it permissible to attach parts of townships to an eligible block regardless of whether they were rectangular or any other shape. That went a long way toward ironing out some of the injustices which had occurred under the act in previous years.
Later, I believe it was two years ago, the government saw fit to amend the act to do away with the irregular block and return to the rectangular block again. Since that time we have again had the experience of some farmers in a township who have had a total crop loss not being able to qualify because there were farmers living near them who had had a fair crop of wheat; and because it is not possible now to attach blocks of sections to the rectangular block they find themselves left out of the act entirely. That is something that must be changed if we are to bring about any kind of justice under that act, particularly in the province of Manitoba.
There is another matter, and that is the part of the act which now denies the benefits of the act to any person who is farming land which he purchased from the provincial government after January 1, 1940, with the exception, of course, of V.L.A. land. There are many farmers in the province of Manitoba, particularly in the northern parts of it which developed rapidly after 1940, who purchased land from the government of Manitoba. This land is quite suitable for growing grain.
These farmers are obliged to pay a levy of 1 per cent on every bushel of grain they market. It is deducted from their grain ticket when they deliver to the elevator; it is not a matter of choice. It is a tax which they are obliged to pay. That money goes into the prairie farm assistance fund. Then after a number of years, after having paid perhaps $2,000 into the fund, when these farmers suffer a crop loss and make application for prairie farm assistance, they are told that under the act, since their land was purchased after January 1, 1940 and it is not V.L.A. land, they are not eligible for prairie farm assistance.

That is a distinct injustice. It is a distinct discrimination. Under any form of crop insurance scheme a thing like that simply could not occur. We know that under any crcp insurance scheme, if a person pays his premium he becomes eligible for compensation in case of loss. That is a fundamental principle of insurance. But under this legislation the government has taken unto itself the right to levy a tax of 1 per cent on every bushel of grain the farmer sells and then to tell him, after he has paid this levy for five, six or ten years, that he is not eligible to collect anything from this fund. It is a one-way street as far as they are concerned. That is another injustice which must be ironed out. It is becoming a major problem in many parts of Manitoba, and many farmers feel strongly on that point.
Those are two of the items that need straightening out under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We would have expected that some action would be taken during the present session of parliament. However, we have been informed by the minister that he has changed his mind and no amendments will be brought down. I hope he will take a second look.
While I am dealing with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act I also want to say this. In the prairie provinces, particularly in the province of Manitoba, which under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has had the experience of having paid into the fund almost three times as much as it has received from it, there is a growing feeling that some other form of insurance is required. But even in the other provinces which we have, percentagewise, fared a little bit better under this act there is growing up a strong demand for some form of crop insurance.
Only two years ago in Manitoba, and earlier than that in the province of Saskatchewan investigations were made into the feasibility of setting up a crop insurance scheme on a provincial basis. The reports of the commissions in both provinces have raised some doubts whether it would be financially possible for a province to underwrite a crop insurance scheme on its own. I think the time is going to come-and it may have to be very soon- when the federal government will have to sit down with the representatives of the three prairie provinces and work out a sound, feasible financial arrangement under which a crop insurance scheme covering the three prairie provinces could be set up in order that every farmer who pays his premium under such a scheme would become eligible for
Supply-Agriculture
compensation in case of crop loss. That is something with regard to which the federal government should take some initiative.
I also want to refer to another act which comes under the Department of Agriculture. I refer to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. At the beginning of this session I had placed on the order paper a resolution calling for the expansion of the present Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act into a sort of Canadian rehabilitation act which would cover all agricultural areas in Canada. We on the prairies are conscious of the fact that there are many other parts of Canada outside the prairie provinces that have problems of reclamation, conservation and drainage, and that there should be something under which these projects could be undertaken.
I want to deal particularly with what are referred to in the estimates as the special projects. These are the projects which are carried out by prairie farm rehabilitation personnel and management but which do not come directly under the terms of the act. They are carried out under a special vote of this parliament. We have had a number of these special projects in the province of Manitoba, and a good part of the work was done in the constituency of Dauphin.
This spring we were greatly disappointed to find that the federal government is backing down or backing away from even the inadequate position it had taken some years ago with regard to these special projects. Until recently the arrangement that had been made was that the federal government would pay 50 per cent of the cost of these special projects having to do with flood control and that the province would share the other 50 per cent with the municipalities. In practice it worked out that, at the beginning, the federal government paid 50 per cent of the cost plus the costs of surveying and engineering, which were carried out by P.F.R.A. personnel and the province paid approximately two-thirds of the other 50 per cent. That left about one-sixth of the cost for the municipalities concerned. Even under that system, and even though a great deal of valuable work was done, it was a heavy burden on the municipalities. In most cases the municipalities which needed these special flood control projects most were least able to pay their part of the cost.

subtopic: FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1954-55 WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT ON GRAIN FOR 1956-57

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Irvin Sluder (Swift Current-Maple
Creek): Mr. Speaker, I wish to submit a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, of which I have given him previous notice, hoping he could, if possible, answer it today.
Is the minister in a position to announce the final payment on wheat through the wheat board for the 1954-55 crop year? Can he also inform us what the initial payment on grain will be during the new 1956-57 crop year?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1954-55 WHEAT-INITIAL PAYMENT ON GRAIN FOR 1956-57
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having received notice of the question I have been able to get certain information and can make a statement to the house concerning three aspects of the western grain marketing situation: one, the final payment on the 1954-55 wheat pool account; two, the policy of the wheat board with respect to delivery quotas during the remainder of the present crop year; three, initial prices for wheat, oats and barley during the crop year which begins August 1 next.
Dealing first with the final payment covering the 1954-55 pool account wheat, I am pleased to be able to advise the house that the Canadian wheat board propose making a cut-off as at May 4, tomorrow, and are recommending to the government a transfer of the unsold stocks, approximately 50 million bushels in amount, to the 1955-56 pool account as at that date. This action will enable the board to close out the 1954-55 pool account.
Total receipts of wheat from producers in this pool amounted to 318,439,061 bushels plus 615,839 bushels purchased from other than producers and 164,055,511 bushels transferred from 1953-54 pool account, a total of 483,110,411 bushels.
As soon as the board's accounts have been completed, I shall be in a position to announce to the house the exact amount of the final payment and the rate per bushel for each grade of grain delivered to the pool. I expect to be in a position to make this announcement about the middle of this month. According

Inquiries of the Ministry to present plans, the wheat board will begin issuing cheques to producers on or about May 22 or 23 and will have completed this final payment about the end of this month of May.
I turn now to policy with respect to delivery quotas at country points. A very heavy movement of wheat and other grain into and out of country elevators is now under way. Deliveries by farmers will increase as road conditions improve and will continue at a high level during the balance of the current crop year. The movement of grain to seaboard is also very heavy. Our export clearances are now reflecting heavy sales commitments entered into in recent months, about which I have previously informed the house. I am not yet in a position to put a firm estimate on export clearances for the whole of the crop year but I can assure hon. members that wheat and flour export clearances will substantially exceed last year's figure of about 252 million bushels.
As a result of this heavy outward movement, the wheat board has been able to increase its grain delivery quotas very substantially in recent weeks. As at May 1 only 14 stations remained on a quota of 1 bushel per specified acre. A 2-bushel quota is in effect at 478 stations. Some 572 stations have a 3-bushel quota, 602 stations a 4-bushel quota and 400 stations a 5-bushel quota. In addition to these basic quotas, supplementary quotas are in effect covering delivery of malting barley, high grade oats, rye and various classes of seed grain. Since the beginning of the season an open quota has been in effect covering the delivery of Durum wheat and flaxseed.
Total grain deliveries since August 1 are now about 300 million bushels and the Canadian wheat board expects that space will be provided at country elevators to enable total farm deliveries * of about 500 million bushels during the crop year. It is expected that wheat deliveries for the whole of the present crop year will exceed 1954-55 but that deliveries of oats and barley will fall somewhat short of last year's figure.
I have, been advised by the board that although they expect that they will be in a position to accept delivery from producers of as much grain as in 1954-55, it may not be possible for them to arrange to equalize deliveries by individual farmers to the extent that this was arranged for during the past two crop years. Hon. members may remember that during last crop year the board endeavoured to provide delivery opportunities to enable all producers to deliver a minimum quota of eight bushels per specified acre. This looked like a feasible target.


However, estimates of potential deliveries at many delivery stations proved to be wide of the mark, and it was not possible for the board to accept all the eight-bushel deliveries prior to July 31. It therefore became necessary for the board to issue special 1955-56 quota delivery permits to enable producers who had not delivered their eight-bushel quota prior to July 31 to complete these deliveries along with new quota deliveries during the current season.
It is always the aim of the board to equalize delivery opportunities in so far as this is possible. The board has advised me, however, that last year the attempt to reach a uniform target did have an adverse effect upon the marketing of Canadian grain in export markets. Much of the grain delivered last fall against the previous year's quota and moved to terminal positions was made up of varieties and grades not needed for immediate marketing requirements. This grain added to the congestion in storage facilities and utilized scarce transportation, thus creating difficulties for the board in moving to seaboard position for immediate clearance those varieties and grades of new crop grain for which there was an immediate and urgent demand.
In the light of this experience the Canadian wheat board have advised me that, if they are to meet market requirements and their forward sales commitments, it may not be possible to attain a uniform quota at all delivery stations during the present crop year.
The primary objective of the board will be to bring forward grain to cover sales commitments or for which there appears to be a ready demand. The board will, however, working with the transport controller, the elevator companies and the railways, continue to endeavour to achieve as high a degree of equality of delivery opportunity as is possible without interfering with the sales objective. The board will increase delivery quotas at individual stations as space is created, but will restrict shipments of grain from higher quota stations to the movement of grain required to meet commitments. In order to avoid the serious situation that arose last year, the wheat board has decided that all quotas in effect as at July 31, 1956, will expire as at that date and deliveries after August 1 will apply against the 1956-57 crop year quotas which will be made effective on August 1.
Although this wheat quota policy may result in some producers in western Canada, at the end of the current crop year, having delivered more grain per specified acre than others, there should be general agreement

that, at a time of intense international competition, the Canadian wheat board must have freedom to give preference to deliveries of the varieties and grades of grain for which there is an immediate demand and that the board cannot afford to pass up market opportunities in an endeavour to equalize farm deliveries between producers.
At this time, I also wish to announce to the house that the government has approved initial prices to be paid by the Canadian wheat board on the basic grades of wheat, oats and barley for the crop year beginning August 1, 1956, at the same level as during the present crop year. These initial prices are as follows:
Wheat-$1.40 per bushel basis No. 1 Manitoba Northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver.
Oats-65 cents per bushel No. 2 Canada Western in store Fort William/Port Arthur.
Barley-96 cents per bushel basis No. 3 Canada Western six-row in store Fort William/Port Arthur.

Supply-Agriculture SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Administration service-
1. Departmental administration (including advisory committee on agricultural services), $670,015.

In taking part in the debate on the agriculture estimates, it is not my intention to take up too much time, and I do not believe I shall take my full allotted time of 30 minutes. Nor shall I give what might be termed a statistical address, offering a multitude of figures that I know few people care to listen to and even fewer people care to read. I shall leave that to the Minister of Agriculture, who is a past master in the art of conglomerating and twisting figures and statistics to suit the immediate occasion. Nobody knows what they are all about; perhaps not even the minister. It all simmers down to a little bit of addition here and a little bit of subtraction there with even some multiplication and division thrown in, and I am sure that in order to make the farmers appear better off than they ever have been he must have used much more addition than subtraction. We have been told of meetings held across western Canada in protest against the government's wheat policy. On reviewing the proceedings and statements made by different members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at their meeting in Hamilton one sees that the same thing could very easily happen in eastern Canada. I should like to quote a few extracts from what was said at that meeting. In the Rural Co-operator of January 31, 1956 I find the following:
The federal minister of agriculture is trying to "make fools out of the farmers of this country'', D. E. Stauffer, a past president of United Cooperatives of Ontario, told the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Hamilton on January 25. Mr. Stauffer urged the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to protest strongly the misleading impressions of farm prosperity given by published reports of a January 23 speech of the Canadian Minister of Agriculture.
Again I quote:
The C.F.A. annual meeting on January 26 approved a statement noting "with regret" that the minister's comparison of cash and net farm income for the most recent five year periods "while technically correct tends to leave an erroneous impression with the public."
I quote further:
"How long is Mr. Gardiner going to be allowed to get away with this kind of thing", Mr. Stauffer asked. "A whole year's work is thrown away when the minister gives statements like that to the press. He does it every year before the C.F.A. meeting, and it's got to stop."

Eastern members have listened very attentively and, I may say, with a great deal of interest and sympathy to the debate with relation to the difficulties of the prairie farmers which has taken up much of the time of the house since January 10. After listening to the debate yesterday on the distribution of box cars I am beginning to wonder whether there has not been a word spoken in the house for every grain of surplus wheat there is in the western provinces.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether we could have a little order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is very difficult to hear the hon. member. At the same time, if he did not refer so extensively to his notes perhaps he might himself command a little better order in the chamber.
Hear, hear.
That is a fine bunch to be applauding.
I am referring to notes and I have noticed that many hon. members on the other side of the house, especially the cabinet ministers on the front bench, refer to notes all the time.
They read their entire speeches.

We fully appreciate the fact that many hundreds of farmers in the three prairie provinces are experiencing very difficult times. It is no secret, it is a known fact to everyone that the whole economy of the west depends on the prosperity of those living in the rural districts and their ability to dispose of their wheat or at least to deliver a sizeable quantity of their crop to the elevator.
From listening to different members and looking over reports concerning the prairies we know that there are many millions of bushels of wheat still on the farm and that many hundreds of farmers have received very little and in some cases no cash for their crop for a year or more. Is it any wonder that the farmers are not only asking for but demanding, although in vain, cash advances on farm stored grain? I admit that guaranteed bank loans will be of some help. That is why we the official opposition supported the resolution; but it will not solve the financial difficulty and stress that many producers find themselves in at the present time. The wheat they have in storage on their farms is in fact equivalent to their hard-earned dollars of the past year, and in some instances for a longer period. No wonder they object to paying interest on

their own money. I have been in communication with many western wheat growers and they seem to be all of the same opinion, regardless of their political affiliations, namely that the wheat board should advance them cash on the grain stored on their farms.
While western agriculturists at the present time are subjected to all this difficulty, that is not saying that everything in eastern Canada is rosy; not by any means. The farmer in eastern Canada-and I have in mind now the dairy farmer-has his many problems owing to reduced revenue and rising cost. The dairy farmers in eastern Canada would and could feed many millions of bushels of western grain if they could get for their milk products a remuneration comparable to the cost of grain they buy. Every farmer is well aware of the fact that if he purchases feed grain at $3 per hundred, which is the price in the east at present, and has been for quite some time, he must receive the same price per hundred for his milk in order to make it profitable for him to purchase. Today the farmer who is producing milk for butter, evaporated or powdered milk or cheese receives from $2 to $2.40 per hundred net. Hence it is utterly impossible for him to buy grain at $3 per hundred and receive an average of approximately $2.25 for his products.
At this time I should like to give some statistics with regard to the price paid in one of the three concentrated milk plants in my own county in order to show the committee the difference in price of milk at the present time as compared with that in 1951. In 1951 the top price in this one particular milk plant was $3.25 per hundred with a low price of $3.15. I am taking the lowest price paid that year. In 1952 the price dropped to $2.75 or a drop of 40 cents per hundred. In 1953 the price dropped again to $2.33 per hundred or a net drop of 82 cents from 1951. In 1954 the price dropped to $2.34 per hundred or a net drop of 81 cents from 1951. In 1955 the price was $2.43 or a drop of 72 cents from 1951.
Taking into consideration the total number of pounds of milk shipped to this milk plant in those four years, the net loss to the shippers to that plant was $1,322,653 or a net loss per year of an average of $330,000.
In my county we have three milk plants of practically comparable size. Therefore the loss to the dairy farmer in Leeds county, or its borders, in the three milk plants is $1 million per year. Cheese also is an important product in my county, as well as in other parts of eastern Canada-as you know, eastern Ontario has the banner cheese-producing county in Canada, Things are not altogether 67509-224
Supply-Agriculture
rosy for the cheese producer either. In 1951 the average price for cheese milk was $2.74 per hundred. In 1952 it was $2.16; in 1953, $2.14; and in 1954, $2.20. When you take into consideration the amount of milk that is purchased in Ontario to make cheese you will see that the loss in those four years was $3,625,200 annually. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, that proves conclusively to me that there has been a reduction in the purchasing power of the dairy farmers of Ontario, particularly of eastern Ontario.
I say to my western friends, if we in the east were to receive a fair and comparable price for our produce we could take care of many, many millions of your western grain surplus. In fact, we would have to increase the grain rations to our herds of cattle by an average of only three or four bushels a day for each farm to take care of a least 50 million bushels of your surplus. I have heard many farmers make the statement that they would like to feed their cattle, especially the dairy cows, more grain but they could not afford to purchase it.
Few people who have not had the experience can visualize the overhead cost of a dairy farmer. He must provide storage for his hay, grain and silage and stables for his cattle. The cost is terrific and now that farm labour is so scarce he must have his farm well-equipped with machinery, not only seeding and harvesting equipment but very expensive machinery for his forage crops such as hay and corn. This runs into many thousands of dollars.
If a young professional man, or a man working in industry at a fair salary or wage, wants to build or purchase himself a house he can get a loan from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation up to 90 per cent of the value, but if a young man wants to purchase a farm he can get a loan of only 60 per cent of the value from the farm loan board. Why is this? Why the discrimination? It must be that the government thinks the earning power of the man in business, or the man who works in industrial plants, is greater and more secure than that of the man on the farm. If this is so, it is about time they gave some consideration to the needs of agriculture so that the earning power of the farmer will be equal to that of people in other walks of life.
A young man may buy a farm now with the ordinary down payment, and by the time he gets it stocked with cattle and equipped with the necessary implements and before the mortgage is discharged, he has paid the equivalent of the amount of the mortgage two or three times in interest and, in many instances, at his death he is compelled to leave a portion of the mortgage for his son

Supply-Agriculture
to finish paying. That has happened quite often. Is it any wonder that the farmers' sons are not staying at home to carry on where their fathers leave off? I hope the time will not come when it will be the survival of the largest. Surely there is a place in our rural districts for small-sized family farms; but I am afraid they are fast disappearing. Why? Because the farmer and his son or help, whichever it may be, on the ordinary farm cannot make his revenue meet his expenses.
Farmers to the number of 205,000 filed income tax returns for 1953 showing an average net income of $2,125. Of this number,
135,000	with an average income of only $1,244 were not taxable. Those who do file income tax returns are the largest and most successful farmers, and yet they earn only an average income of $2,125. But that is not all. We must realize that it is not the farmer or the head of the house, who earns this income; it is the earnings of the whole family, his wife and family combined. I think it is high time that the farmer's wife, who works long hours on the farm and helps her husband and looks after the family, should be allowed $250 as an exemption in income tax as are other wives who work in offices, shops or factories.
Then, there is the smaller farmer, his wife and family, who are earning an average of only $1,244 or less. A man who is slightly handy can go down town and buy himself a hammer, a saw and an old rusty square and earn far more as a carpenter's helper, working only eight hours a day, five days a week, than he can on the farm at the present time.
Whenever the Minister of Agriculture speaks he always averages the years 1951, 1952, 1953, 1954 and 1955. He is very careful not to present the economic picture of the last three years when the net farm income declined around 60 per cent. I have a machine price list in my hand. In 1941 a binder could be purchased for $253.50. At the present time anybody who has had anything to do with farming and with farm machinery knows that the price has more than doubled. At the present time we pay $550 for a binder. There has been an increase from $253.50 in 1941 to $550 at the present time. That goes for all. kinds of machinery that the farmer must buy to carry on his farming activities. It is not so much the number of dollars a farmer owns, it is the purchasing power of those dollars that count.
In 1901 the farm population was 45 per cent of the total population. In 1951 it was only 19 per cent. But the lamentable part
[Mr. Stanton.1
of the story is that 19 per cent of our population today is receiving only 6-8 per cent of our gross national income, which is out of all proportion. In fact, from 1951 to 1954 the farmer's share of the gross national income has dropped from 13-6 per cent to 6-8 per cent, and still the minister has the audacity to tell the house and every public meeting that he addresses that there is nothing wrong with agriculture.
There were more unpaid taxes in the rural municipalities of eastern Ontario in 1955 than there had been for many years, and I presume that is true of all farming districts of Canada. Also, many grocery and hardware stores in the rural villages are going on a cash basis, which is a very good criterion of the diminishing purchasing power of the farmers.
It has been so long since eastern Canada has had a minister of agriculture that we in the east are beginning to wonder whether the minister is of the opinion that there are no farmers in the east at all. I believe we have not had a minister of agriculture in eastern Canada since 1911. If the Conservative party does not appoint one from eastern Canada after the next election-surely we are entitled to one in every 50 years-they will certainly hear from me.
The heads of the different agricultural associations have been doing a wonderful job in creating better public relations between the urban and rural districts. They have gone a long way in dispelling the suspicion that the farmer was getting too much for his products. Now the minister runs around telling how well off the farmers are, how much better off they are now than they were years ago. He does more harm in one of his speeches that is broadcast on the radio and printed in the press than the public relations association can rectify in a whole year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And he does it just about once a week.

Mr. Chairman, in my constituency we have a very large turkey industry at the present time although I would not say it is thriving because we do not have ample protection for poultry, especially turkeys. If the duty were sufficient to protect the turkey growers in Canada, it would expand into one of the great industries of this country, consuming much of the surplus grain that the prairies have at the present time.
In 1954, Canada imported over 5 million pounds of turkey from the United States; in 1955 she imported double that, or 10 million pounds. Now, what do we have in 1956? Up until February 11, the market report shows imports of 422,000 pounds, and for the same period in 1955 it was 96,000 pounds.

The official prediction from the United States department of agriculture is for an increase of 6 per cent in turkeys raised this year. With the Canadian tariff as it is, at 124 per cent ad valorem, if there were a break in the United States market owing to the tremendous amount of turkeys being raised this year the duty might well drop to three or four cents per pound.
I think that the turkey growers, of whom there are now a considerable number in Leeds county-and there will be more if they are adequately protected-are not asking for too much when they suggest that the tariff should be 12i per cent ad valorem, but not less than five cents per pound.
Under the present tariff, turkeys may come into Canada at a very low tariff when the price is lowest in the United States, and this may have a very damaging effect on our market here. The farmers are reasonable when they ask for protection only comparable to other industries in Canada. This they must have, if they are going to survive and play their part in expanding this country in the next fifty years, making it the great nation that we all visualize.
It is time the government woke up to the fact and admitted that all is not well with our basic industry. It is time it realized that there should be more equality in the distribution of our gross national income. Surely the government must realize that much of our present industrial prosperity can be attributed to credit buying. Without a very strong agricultural economy, I hesitate to imagine where this whole Canadian economy may drift.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on item No. 1 of the agriculture estimates and though I think my remarks will primarily be of interest to hon. members from the province of Ontario some of the topics which I discuss will no doubt be of interest to all the farmers in Canada.

This would give the farmers some idea of the quantity of stock that is being handled and at what price that stock is being sold.
I feel there is great merit in this recommendation. I realize that these broadcasts are not paid for by our government but are handled as a news item, but I believe that the
